Character customization in GTA has never been so good, and you even have two characters to fit this time around, meaning there are more choices than ever when picking Jason and Lucia's GTA 6 outfits, tattoos, and hairstyles.

You may have already seen just a few of the countless variants for Lucia's hair doing the rounds on socials, but since different shops and stylists offer different options, it's not always easy to find what you're after. That's where we come in. This is our growing list of our favorite GTA 6 outfits, including exactly where to pick them up for yourself, so make sure you have enough cash to spend by checking out our guide to the best ways to get money fast in GTA 6, then go shopping.

The best hairstyles and colors for Lucia can usually be found in the Signature section at specific stylists, as this is where unique styles can be found that you can't just find everywhere.

Check out these styles and where to get them below:

You've probably seen this Spiky Twin Buns style online as it seems to be the crowd-favorite Lucia style, and it can be found in the Signature section at Clip & Fade in Stockyard, Vice City. While this looks great with a solid hair color, I personally love this look with the pink color, as the contrast between Lucia's warm brunette roots and the bright pink spiky buns looks super cool. You can get this pink ombre dye at Pearl Hair Salon in Port Gellhorn.

If you prefer something a bit more natural and cultural, then give these gorgeous Goddess Box Braids a go - they're a very popular style right now. While I'd usually opt for a pop of color in Lucia's hair (to counter all that black I've got her wearing), this style best suits a nice warm brunette. You can get this in a few places, but I'd recommend Crosstown Cutz in, well, Crosstown, Vice City.

For something a little more sophisticated, try out this slicked back bun and forehead curl look with a platinum blonde or a deep, dark brown. This might be a style you want to try out for a night on the town rather than a bank heist or a day car jacking, but each to their own. Head to the stylist at Crosstown Cutz in Vice City to try it out.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

My personal favorite hairstyle for Lucia, though, is this wavy high ponytail and braids look that you can also get from Clip & Fade (can you figure out my top salon pick, yet?). Not only does it looks absolutely amazing on our female protagonist, but it shows off the incredible GTA 6 hair physics better than any other hairstyle I've seen yet.

While this style suits any color, I particularly think it looks great in a bright shade, so go for this Intense Red, again available at Clip & Fade, or the pink from above.

It's very worth noticing the cool detail that Lucia's make-up smudges if she stays up too long without getting it touched up. This is more obvious in cut scenes than just exploring surroundings, so make sure you've got the best make-up on before starting a new mission.

To make Lucia's make up stand out, it's worth picking something with a bright lip or bold eye. This Classic Vinewood look checks that first box with a super glossy red lip and a subtle smokey eye. Get it at Hair by Clair in Capri.

This one's a bit subtler on first glance, but on closer inspection, you'll see a cute smattering of gold stars lining Lucia's eyes, leading to this look's name: Celestial. What first drew me to this looks, though, was the gorgeous coral lipstick, and if you like it too, you can get it at Salon Belle in Rockridge.

Finally, this strong, smoky, retro look perfect compliments Lucia's attitude and many of her best outfits. I particularly love the dark liner - it's time that look came back. You can also find this look at Salon Belle in Rockridge.

My favorite nail art options for Lucia are:

Honestly, my favorite nails for Lucia are the retro Glossy Red Nails that can be picked up anywhere, but only with the Vintage Vice City Pack. This was a pre-order bonus, so you might already have it, but you can purchase the pack separately if not. With the pack, you can get this set anywhere that does nails, but you'll need to tab across to the 'Special Nails' menu.

If you don't have the Vintage Vice City pack and don't want to fork out real-life cash for a set of virtual nails, then I also love this long tortoiseshell set you can get from Salon Belle in Rockridge. It's tricky to find this salon, as it's located inside a residential block, but once you do, you can get these nails in long or short variants, as well as a load of other unique hair and nail designs.

These are my top picks for Jason's hair and facial hair in GTA 6:

Honestly, Jason's standard haircuts are some of his best, and you can get those at any salon. Personally, I switch between this mid-length wavy slick back style and the long slick back style. You can always tweak the color to make it a bit more interesting, for example with a dusty blue bye from Pearl Hair Salon in Port Gellhorn or a bright pink or green from Clip & Fade.

Some good signature styles can be found for Jason, though, and this Short Slick Back look at Hair by Clair in Capri is among them, as one of the nicer shorter styles I've seen.

Look, sometimes, you may as well fit in with the locals, and there's no better way of doing that in the Port Gellhorn area than with a good old mullet. Whether or not you want to change it up by the time you get to Vice City is up to you, but you'll find this iconic style at Pearl Hair Salon in south Port Gellhorn.

Selecting and showcasing the best outfits for Lucia is a near impossible task, honestly, as there are just so many options out there. However, I've listed a few of my personal favorites below to give a brief snapshot of what's on offer and what each store stocks.

For a cool, casual day-to-night outfit, I just love this look on Lucia. These pants are my absolute go-to since they look great paired with any bodysuit or crop top (I'm also a big fan of the red high-neck bodysuit from location). However, you're not going to get away with an underboob crop top quite this short in real life without constant anxiety of a wardrobe malfunction, so I figure why not wear one when you know it's not going anywhere. You could always put something over the top until it's time to hit clubs if you're feel self-conscious.

Okay, I like wearing black, and that seems to be a trait I'm forcing onto Lucia, too, but that doesn't mean you have to. The bodysuit I've paired with the skirt above only comes in a black, but there are other similar one-pieces available in red, purple, and even leopard print, if that's your thing. Check them out at the back of Ferruccio Tucci stores.

Similarly, this gorgeous thigh-split skirt comes in other colors too, making them look more like beach wear, while this soft black can comfortably be worn in any environment. Sadly, I can't remember where I picked the skirt up, but as soon as I find it again, I'll update you here.

This one again is part of the Vintage Vice City pack, but how could I not include it as one of Lucia's best looks. It's a no-brainer - Lucia looks great alongside Jason in his equivalent fit, and they both work it particularly well against a classic GTA 6 car like the Dundreary Chino. Just get that beaut kitted out at your local mod shop, and you'll be ready to ride around Leonida in style.

Provided you've got the Vintage Vice City pack, you can unlock this look at any clothing retailer marked with a yellow price tag. You'll have to equip the hair and make-up separately, but you can do both at most hair salons.

Finally, you can't go wrong with a cute grungy outfit for Lucia, and this pair of baggy jeans from Mid is among the easiest pieces to team with any of her cute top options. One of my favorites, though, is this bandana top from Aline's Thrift Store in La Perle. Finally, get Lucia a pair of comfy Vans-style slip-ons from Mid to finish of the look.

As with Lucia, there are far too many options to choose from, so here's just a few options to inspire and to give an example of what different stores have to offer.

Slater are denim specialists, and you'll even be able to pick up this ready-made outfit in their stores across Leonida. It's a classic American look, and if you want to go all Justin and Britney on us, you can pick up a matching denim look for Lucia while you're there.

Unlike with Lucia, I like to put a bit more color into Jason's clothes, and I love this combo that just screams classic Floridian - I mean Leonidian - smart casual. You'll be able to pick up the knit shirt from the This That chain of stores, while the green pants can be found in any of the Nola branches across Vice City. Both offer a variety of smart-casual garments for both Jason and Lucia. I'm still not sold on this particular pair of shoes, though, so have a browse for a pair you like. Footwear can be found in both clothes stores and dedicated shoe shops, so there's plenty of choice.

There's nothing quite like rocking up to a bank robbery looking this suave - no one's expecting you to pull out a pistol in an outfit like this. You can pick up a suit for both Jason and Lucia at Ferruccio Tucci formalwear stores across the map, though Lucia's don't look as good. Instead, browse the bodysuits for her while you're here.

Finally, we've gone for a casual rocker look, mainly thanks to this t-shirt and jacket found at Aline's Thrift Store in La Perle. Team them with some jeans and either some boots or a pair of Vans knock offs from Mid, then complete the look with headphones from any local tech shop.

If you're working on keeping your GTA 6 relationship status high, then you might want to consider getting matching tattoos with your beau. There aren't many of these, and one is locked behind a special side quest, but I can't get enough of this 'In this Life...' '...and the next' pair. This is another one I've had equipped for a while and can't quite remember where I got it, but I'm looking, and I'll update you here when I find it.

We've got loads more GTA 6 guides, so check them out if you're looking for more help as you explore Leonida.

#3796. Rockstar Games reveals 23 extra tracks in GTA 6's deluxe edition soundtrack, featuring Denzel Curry, HEALTH, and more

For those of you out there in love with Grand Theft Auto 6's soundtrack, you'll be happy to know that Rockstar Games have revealed an additional 23 tracks as part of the game's deluxe edition album.

These tracks, available via streaming services, include songs from artists like HEALTH, Denzel Curry, Playboi Carti, and more. You can find the full track list on the official Rockstar Games music website.

Some of these artists played a significant role in the game. Justice, for example, helped compose the game's original soundtrack and several of their tracks appear throughout the game. There are others, too.

Both Sexyy Red and Denzel Curry voice characters in the game's later chapters. Others like Kodack Black and Freddie Gibbs also show up, too - that's not to mention the huge number of musicians who make an appearance in the game's many radio stations. If you listen through those, you'll hear the voices of Keith Richards, Lana Del Ray, The Alchemist and others.

Musical talent also played an additional role in creating the TV advertisements and shows you can watch in the game. Zack Fox is one example, as is Weird Al Yankovic. Both wrote parts of the game's enticing and absurd big screen entertainment - which makes sense given the pair's shared comedy background.

Gigabyte's Gaming A16 laptop with the RTX 5070 and 16GB DDR5 RAM is one of the cheapest that comes equipped with that particular GPU. At 1200p, even the 85W RTX 5070 gets plenty of room to stretch its legs, and 1TB of storage is pretty sweet - it lets you go nuts during quite a few Steam sales.

Key specs: RTX 5070 (85 W) | Ryzen 7 260 | 16-inch | 1200p | 165 Hz | 16 GB DDR5 | 1 TB SSD

Price check: Walmart $1,549.99 (Core Ultra 9 185H) | Amazon $1,448 (Core i7-13620H)

How are we all doing, fellow Black Friday shoppers? Feeling the evil clutches of the memory crisis closing in? Crying over $2,000 GPUs? Having nightmares about laptop prices?

Well, I can't help you with the clutches and whatnot, but I can certainly help you with a great Black Friday gaming laptop deal today. I just spotted this Gigabyte Gaming A16 laptop at Best Buy, and when I saw those specs with that price tag, I felt a (brief, fleeting, but much-needed) sense of relief. Now there is a decent laptop at a reasonable price. So they do exist.

Gigabyte's Gaming A16 has a bunch of things worth mentioning, but the best part is certainly the Nvidia RTX 5070 GPU. That's a midrange GPU at what is now an almost budget-level price, so it's genuinely a good deal. The caveat here is that it's the 85 W version, so it's not the most powerful iteration of the RTX 5070 you'll ever get to see, but at this price? I'll take it.

Apart from the RTX 5070, which, with the help of DLSS 5, should be able to carry most games at reasonable settings, you're also getting the AMD Ryzen 7 260 laptop CPU, a 1 TB SSD, and 16 GB DDR5 RAM. Display-wise, we're looking at a 1920 x 1200 resolution with a 165 Hz refresh rate. All in all, very respectable.

Shopping now, during Black Friday sales, gives you $300 off the regular list price. That's a whole lot of laptop for just $1,300, so I'd jump on this deal while it's still up.

But wait... 16 GB DDR5 RAM sounds a little bit restrictive, right? It's what we're used to in this hellscape, what with the memory shortages, but it's not ideal. Well, good news, Best Buy also has a 32 GB DDR5 version of that same-ish laptop. It's not the exact same, but it's pretty close, and the best part is that it's still affordable.

Gigabyte's Gaming A16 laptop is the cheapest way to bag yourself an RTX 5070 mobile GPU, even if it is a restricted version at 85 W. But with this slight extra expense you also get a full 32 GB of DDR5 memory. And that is worth way more than the ~$80 extra this costs over the 16 GB machine.

Key specs: RTX 5070 (85 W) | Core i7-13620H | 16-inch | 1200p | 165 Hz | 32 GB DDR5 | 1 TB SSD

Price check: Walmart $1,618 | Amazon $1,618

This model brings you over to Intel with the Core i7-13620H mobile chip, but it keeps the RTX 5070 (85W) and the 1200p 165Hz screen. It fixes my main issue with the cheaper model without ramping up the price too much. And for a premium that is considerably lower than it would be if you were to try and upgrade the $1,300 version yourself.

The 32 GB version of the Gigabyte Gaming A16 is now $1,379, down from $1,849.99, at Best Buy. Scoop it up while it's still there and enjoy having a solid GPU at what's now a reasonable price.

#3793. AI-generated GTA 6 PC ports get nuked in alleged Rockstar takedown spree, as former Bungie dev hails "most ridiculous dumpster fire ever"

3007 Github repos allegedly DMCA'd at a stroke

One of the creators of an unofficial AI-generated PC "port" of Grand Theft Auto 6 claims that Rockstar and Take-Two Interactive have already stepped in to shut down the project, though the fearful work of slop-and-pasting GTA 6 to PC appears to be continuing in other hands. Titled "Leonida", after the game's setting, the port is a recompilation – that is, a translation of the game's original code into code that'll run natively on different hardware, rather than being live translated by an emulator as you play. It's based on an incomplete GTA 6 Xbox build of the game, including the all-important executable file, which was leaked earlier in the week by crypto grifter Cyberleek.

As documented by former Bungie developer Amy Hendricks in an increasingly depressed Bluesky thread (excerpt: "This is the most ridiculous dumpster fire ever"), Leonida is or was being made using Claude and Google's Antigravity tools. Going by Hendricks's posts, which are based on watching a Leonida stream, much of the recomp's creation seems to have consisted of one or more high school kids typing prompts like "work faster", while spending hundreds or thousands of dollars in usage fees.

The Leonida team appear to have succeeded in getting the game to boot on PC, but two key members, NotRexed and Shayder, have now withdrawn from the project and scrubbed any mention of it from their social media feeds.

In posts preserved by cheery RPS fanzine PCGamer, NotRexed shared a snapshot of a copyright infringement takedown notification from Discord. They explained their decision to call it quits as follows: "Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I’ve said before, I’m a 15 year old kid. Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on Discord." I myself am a middle aged man, but don't despair, NotRexed! I am not going to yell at you. I am simply going to reach for a moderately small violin.

As reported by PCG, the Leonida Discord server has now been shut down, and the Github repository for the recompilation's code has been nuked. Hendricks has shared an alleged takedown request from a representative of Take-Two Interactive, according to which Github have taken action against 3,007 forks (that is, duplicates for the purposes of making a separate version) from the original Leonida repo. Meanwhile, somebody has set up a leaderboard to chart the progress of several other GTA 6 recomp projects. I'm sure Take-Two's IP enforcement teams appreciate their efforts.

A few days prior to GTA 6's release on console last week, Rockstar North's former tech director Obbe Vermeij told RPS that the GTA makers would release the PC version sooner than anticipated to avoid losing any cash to generative AI rip-offs. IGN subsequently asked Take-Two's CEO Strauss Zelnick for his thoughts on this. Zelnick replied that the company are "not in the least cavalier" about the risk, but are confident people would rather play the game as Rockstar intended.

Affordable wired gaming headsets that work on the Switch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you want your Nintendo Switch 2 to sound as good as possible, you won't dream of using the handheld's built-in stereo speakers, and will pick up a headset to use with the system. It won't cost you much to do so, with Black Friday deals cutting cost on gaming-designed headphones.

There are loads of Black Friday gaming headset deals at Currys, with the best reducing models down to lovely tempting prices. Some are discounted to below £50, which means they're cheaper than the cost of a Switch 2 game. They're all wired models, as cable-toting tech is generally cheaper, which means these options still offer some impressive specs despite the low price. In particular there are four headsets below this price threshold which work on the Switch 2, and you can find them below, ordered from cheapest to priciest.

This wired Logitech gaming headset is over 50% off, despite its specs. It offers 7.1 sound, and is certified as a DTS Headphone:X headphone. It's pretty simple in terms of features, but it's a simple way of getting wired audio from your Switch (or any other console).

This gaming headset is roughly a year old, so is starting to see discounts. It gives you an affordable way to experience some of Turtle Beach's popular audio features, and it's pretty lightweight compared to rivals too.

HyperX offers a fair few gaming headsets we recommend, but thanks to the discount, this is perhaps the cheapest. It's surprisingly cheap when you consider it has dual drivers, offering sonic nuance many alternatives miss.

Coming just under the £50 threshold is this alternative HyperX model, which has a wider range of connection options than the above model and has a more durable frame. It's also designed to be comfortable with soft leatherette padding and memory foam cushions.

The main appeal of almost any gaming headset is thus: dedicated cans will sound better than the tinny loudspeakers you get in a handheld console. The presence of a proper microphone is a benefit too, if you play online with people.

If you usually play your Switch 2 on your home TV, while it's docked, you might not therefore need a gaming headset. Maybe your TV's built-in speakers, or the loudspeakers or soundbar you use for it, work just as well.

I'd therefore recommend a headset mostly to people who play their Switch 2 on the go. In many situations, you can't play your Switch out loud in the first place, so a headset is important, especially since all cans block out surrounding noise by virtue of their padded ear cushions.

But what about cheap versus expensive headsets? Honestly, I think pricey cans are best suited to competitive esports players who need to hear everything around them, or PC gamers who'll have much better access to the headphone software. Usually, what you're paying for is an elite roster of tools, features and preset EQ modes, and it's often hard to play around with those tools if you're not on a computer.

So for most buyers, a budget pair of cans like this is perfect, because audio quality is often the one thing you're not compromising on. The only thing you might want, that costs more, is a wireless connection. If you don't like the idea of using a physical cable, maybe you should pay a little bit more, but convenience is the only benefit to a Bluetooth connection in gaming headsets.

#3791. More than 39 million people have played GTA 6 on PlayStation alone, Sony says, as the game breaks all-time player numbers on the platform

Sony's revealed staggering statistics relating to the popularity of Grand Theft Auto on PlayStation 5, not least that more than 39 million unique people have played the game there. That's more than the official GTA 6 day-one sales tally of 32.5m copies across all platforms.

Unsurprisingly, with such massive numbers, GTA 6 is a record-breaker on PlayStation. According to the PlayStation Blog, the game has recorded the highest number of concurrent players on PlayStation ever, surpassing any previous record across all kinds of game - multiplayer, free-to-play and single-player.

In addition, PlayStation also saw "the largest number of newly connected PS5 consoles on a single day" since the console's launch, outside of end-of-year holidays, suggesting that Rockstar's latest game, more than any other PS5 game released so far, has driven hardware sales. GTA 6 is apparently the first game played on 70 percent of new PS5 consoles.

The average GTA 6 playtime, per person, is a considerable 17.4 hours, the blog says, and the total number of hours spent playing the game is 683 million - a number so high I can't contextualise it.

Microsoft hasn't announced equivalent data for Xbox but I assume the game is a record-breaker there, too, given that it broke pre-order Xbox Store records in the same way GTA 6 did on PlayStation. However, GTA 6 is estimated to have sold far more copies on PlayStation - as many as 75 percent of its total sales, according to Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott.

Elliott estimated that GTA 6 amassed a colossal 44.9m sales by the end of its opening weekend, and that 33.7m of those were on PlayStation 5 (which still doesn't reach the '39 million unique players' stat Sony has just trotted out) and 11.2m were on Xbox. That amount of sales would earn Rockstar something like $4bn in revenue.

The arrival of GTA 6 has, then, been seismic. The game has wowed critics and dominated conversation not only in the games industry but also across entertainment news and mainstream news. Meanwhile, however, we await the verdict in the Rockstar Games employment tribunal in Scotland, relating to the sudden firing of 34 employees a year ago. Was Rockstar union-busting, as alleged? It'll be a historic ruling if deemed so.

#3790. Delivering "a more modern Garry's Mod" is the goal of spiritual successor S&box's revamped sandbox mode, as classic GMod's workshop addon system returns

"I thought that spawning from the cloud was better...but I was wrong"

Facepunch Studios continue to work on S&box, the mix of open source game development platform and Garry's Mod spiritual successor they released to mixed reviews earlier this year. That rough start has it in need of a redemption arc, which the Rust devs are hoping will be powered by going free-to-play and making changes like the revamp of sandbox mode they've just rolled out.

"This new system isn't really new," Newman wrote. "It's the exact same system that Garry's Mod uses. I hold my hands up here, I thought that spawning from the cloud was better...but I was wrong. There definitely is something a lot nicer about installing a big model pack and then having everything right there. I'm sorry it took me so long to come around to realising this."

Similarly, in terms of the updated sandbox mode, Newman noted he feels the team have been "walking the line of making a more modern Garry's Mod really well". "I'm excited by all the possibilities of it," he continued. "Obviously there aren't a ton of addons right now but what we do have is showing a LOT of potential, and that's only going to grow. I've been going through improving things that feel outdated or stupid. I'm resisting bending it all too far, I want it to stay kind of familiar for everyone, but I think we can improve a few things in our new engine."

A number of old school sandbox props, such as chunks of robotics, wheels, gears, and hunks of steel girder are on their way back, while Facepunch are finally ready to add in water. "It has waves," Newman wrote of the latter. "The physics objects get tossed around in the waves. You can go underwater, and swim, and there's caustics and fog and particles and post process effects and stuff." Also, NPCs now "live directly in the engine" making it easier to set up a fight club.

A simplified menu and a whole bunch of performance and dev-focused tweaks round out this update, so go through the full notes if you're keen to read about the likes of workshop mounts and VRAM fragmentation.

As of writing, S&box is still yet to go free-to-play, a change Newman and co previously said is coming "towards the end of the year". If it can nail recapturing the classic GMod magic with updates that players actually want, I think it stands a chance of a comeback. However, as its lifespan thus far has proven, it's harder to rely on high quality user-made games within a game than ever before in an age when people can just resort to using generative AI for an ever-increasing number of things.

53 million puts it above any Call of Duty game

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Analyst estimates have put GTA 6 at 53 million copies sold, which, if accurate, places it as the 13th best-selling game of all time after just a week.

In the least surprising bit of news of 2026, GTA 6 is selling pretty well. It was probably the most anticipated game ever and is the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic, so naturally the sales have followed. The first official number from Rockstar Games placed it at 32.5 million copies sold before it was even released, which had made it the 30th best-selling game ever above the likes of Super Mario Odyssey, Monster Hunter World, and Elden Ring. But that was just pre-release, so it's no shock to say that its fortunes haven't ended there.

Alinea Analytics' head of market analysis, Rhys Elliott, posts the latest estimate over on Twitter, which places Rockstar's latest at 53 million copies sold, making $4.7 billion in its first week.

If this number is accurate, GTA 6 is the 13th best-selling game ever, with it unseating Animal Crossing: New Horizons, and overtaking the likes of Cyberpunk 2077, The Sims, and the Pokemon Generation 1 games (which have a combined sales figure of 47.44 million across Red, Blue and Yellow).

GTA 6 has sold 53M copies (75.7% on PS5) after a week on the market (@alineaanalytics estimates). Some other quick stats from our estimates: - It's made $4.7B (76.1% on PS5, due to regional prices) - 7M players have already played for over 50 hours. - 250K folks have played for over 100 hours (!!!!) - The US accounts for 33.5% of PS5's GTA 6 copies. Publishing another big deep dive on Substack shortly.November 27, 2026

Elliott's data also estimates that just under a quarter of GTA 6 sales were on Xbox, with the Series X|S version accounting for 13 million vs PS5's 40 million. And it's not like it's just selling well either, as he reckons that seven million players have already played over 50 hours, with 250k of those having already played 100 hours. For reference, the game had been out in New Zealand around 219 hours at the time the tweet was posted.

Obviously, this is massively impressive no matter how you look at it. But it's worth keeping in mind that the PC release hasn't even dropped yet, so this has the potential to skyrocket once more when PC players – and console players who are going to double dip – get their hands on it.

#3786. GTA 6 players are already starting to get very good at heists, despite all the new challenges Rockstar has added to the game

Grand Theft Auto 6 has been out for a little while now, and already players are showing off their skills when it comes to the game's many heists. Despite the challenges in getting away clean, some are proving it's possible.

For one, sneaking into a bank while the vault is open and stuffing your bags full of marked bills is a tricky process of gradually making your way through rooms and taking out guards as quietly as possible. While the police in the clip below were called to an eventual breakout of violence, a lengthy getaway allowed for a cheeky payday of almost $100,000 in cash.

This crew really cracked a whole bank vault and walked out with almost $100K in GTA 6 💰🏦🚔😮‍💨 #gtavi #gta pic.twitter.com/pJyFXREBvY

One especially impressive element of Grand Theft Auto 6 is how many of its little mechanics interact with each other. As you can see below, if you bring a vehicle with a winch to a cash machine, you can actually pull it off the wall and drag it away from the scene of the crime.

Why rob a bank in GTA 6 when you can just take the whole ATM💸 How to do it❓- Hook the ATM up to a vehicle with a winch- Drag it through the streets until the cash cases fall out- Shoot them open and get out fast, the cops come quickly!(via u/MelloYello917) pic.twitter.com/5eXbULJWP3

As you progress through Grand Theft Auto 6, the game actually introduces you to both styles of heists. Without spoiling exactly how this happens, you're told how to go about taking on such criminal ventures, and you can continue to do so throughout the game at your pleasure. Still, even after you've been tutorialised, pulling off one of these heists is no joke, and can easily turn chaotic.

This GTA 6 robbery sequence was CRAZY, I couldn't even think straight . pic.twitter.com/l65xSFRoSr

Here's a little tip for those of you looking to pull off a heist yourself. You're told that safety deposit boxes can be rifled through for additional loot. However, when you actually make your way into a vault, these will be closed without much sign on which you can access. If you use the focus mode (by pushing in both L3 and R3), it will highlight boxes which you can shoot open. This, of course, may garner unwanted attention, so whether or not you think it's worth doing is part of the risk/reward dilemma you'll have to reckon with. As is the case with so much stuff in GTA 6 including, but not limited to, car-jacking.

#3785. "More than just war and peace": Total War: Medieval 3's diplomacy system will build on Three Kingdoms' backstabbing, with rulers who aren't just focused on you

Competing claims, new negotiation options, and evolving agendas

Creative Assembly's Total War: Medieval 3 is going to do a lot more with diplomacy, the developers promise. Diplomacy! The soul of any Total War game. They're going to build on the example of Total War: Three Kingdoms, which does allow for some gratifying backroom dealing, in fairness. During my first Thringdoms runthrough, I played Cao Cao, a ruler gifted with the ability to hypnotise people into liking him while hating each other. I spent many idle hours instigating proxy wars. Medieval 3 is apparently going to take all that to "new heights". It is going to make Han politicking seem as sophisticated as texting "get your filthy hands off my bae" to everybody you know on Valentine's Day.

Specifically, Creative Assembly want to create a sense of factions with autonomous agendas and evolving intentions, while placing more stress on questions of geography.

In a blog, game director Pawel Wojs hails Three Kingdoms as "a game defined by its dynamic use of diplomacy, where coalitions, alliances and relationships between characters and factions could fundamentally change the course of a campaign." He continues: "We want to build on those foundations, taking what worked well and exploring how we can push it further for the Medieval world."

As regards "believable agendas", Creative Assemble want the campaign AI to display both a survival instinct and the ability to "pursue its own interests instead of primarily being an antagonist to the player". These agendas will span the game's Politics, Economy, and Families systems, with dynastic considerations affecting behaviour. They want you to be able to read another ruler's intent by tracking back through their past actions. They want weaker factions to sue for peace or seek sensible alliances, rather than "stubbornly being entrenched in a war it is bound to lose". Aww, but I love it when Scotland does that.

The game will aim for a balance of long-term thinking and opportunism, with AI leaders pouncing on short-term prospects even as they keep the whole in mind. And then there are inconvenient "ripple effects": you might get involved with a neighbouring succession crisis because you don't want to deal with the fallout if, you know, That Guy takes the throne.

Speaking of borders, Creative Assembly also want would-be treaty-makers to think harder about terrain and transportation. "For example: You finally reach a faraway realm with your diplomat, opening diplomatic relations to a realm far beyond your initial sphere of influence," Wojs goes on. "Relations are positive, but meaningless due to the lack of physical proximity. Once that faraway realm has access to a port, a trade route can finally be established. This leads to an exchange in culture and trade, and may finally allow you to recruit foreign units into your service."

I have to say, I do find a lot of this language either broadly familiar from previous Twars, or too general to reveal much. There is, however, a closing in-game anecdote from principal designer Thomas Schut that digs into the detail. Schut gives the example of you sending a diplomat to negotiate a 10 year non-aggression pact greased by recognition of another ruler's royal title, in return for their vassalage. Sending a diplomat allows you to negotiate on the spot, but if you'd rather not spare a diplomat, you can also dispatch sealed letters at the price of not being able to see and respond immediately to the other faction's reaction.

Rulers can make public claims to cities, calling on other rulers to support them. Simply conquering and annexing them will damage your standing in every court. You can also forge claims to cities, if only as insurance against wanting to own them someday. Get enough rulers to back you, and you'll be able to throw around grander pronouncements about what you're divinely entitled to. You are the Emperor of Everything! Coalitions will apparently form and fragment over years, old friends turning on each other as their dark plots come to light.

The joy of Cao Cao puppetry notwithstanding, I don't play Total War for the chance to thrash out cunning pacts with bots. I am here to put my archers behind my spearfolk - and hope the other side's cavalry don't notice the cutthroats I've stationed in the woods. I'm more interested in what I've read about Medieval 3's regional levies system. Still, it does sound like Creative Assembly are serious about giving you things to do besides putting other wannabe kings to the sword.

I've lost count of how many times I've settled down to play a brand-new game on Steam, only to be smacked in the face with a giant popup telling me to "Grab a controller and kick back!" instead of using my humble mouse and keyboard.

Thankfully for me I live in a multi-platform household, meaning a controller is never far out of reach. But I've also got staunch PC pals without a pad to pick up and who, rightly enough, don't want to fork out the kinda cash that PlayStation's DualSense or the Xbox controller require.

But I'm a firm believer that a good controller is a must-have tool in a PC gamer's repertoire these days, and we needn't immediately seek out the big names when it comes to a comfortable, robust gamepad. Tons of budget-friendly options have popped up on the market over the years, and while some of them are admittedly pretty naff there are also a bunch of great controllers that won't break the bank.

In fact, I've got three of 'em for under $25 for you right here. That's a third of the price of a DualSense controller! While they don't come with fancy haptics and adaptive triggers, they do offer stick-drift resistant, low-latency gaming. Which, as fun as the bells as whistles can be, are really the most important bits.

A new and improved version of the original Nova Lite, the Nova Lite 2 has Hall effect everything, 1000 Hz polling, and trigger locks. It even has a mechanical D-pad, which is absurd for the money, really.

Key specs: Wireless (Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz) | Asymmetric | Hall effect

Out of the three choices, our pad professional James Bentley tells me he likes the GameSir Nova Lite 2 the best, currently going for $23 at Walmart. It boasts comfort, decent polling, and Hall effect—so much better protection against that pesky stick drift. It's also got our highest review score out of the bunch thanks to its affordability, mechanical d-pad, and choice of 2.4Ghz and Bluetooth.

It's not got great grip, however, and its budget is felt in the less-than-stellar plastic and rather simple software. But for the price you're paying? It's a great, basic choice for those who only need to reach for a controller occasionally.

We've already raved about Hall effect joysticks and how they spell the end for the dreaded stick drift. In this wireless gaming controller, they're a welcome feature, but this handful of gaming hardware packs a few quirky surprises too. For instance, there are extra bumper buttons.

Key specs: Hall effect sticks, triggers | 2.4G wireless | 19 h battery

Price check: Best Buy $21.99 (Black) | Walmart $29.99 (Purple)

But if you're someone who's accustomed to the likes of the Switch Pro controller, you might find the 8BitDo Ultimate 2C a better fit, currently going for $20 at Amazon. It's got a pretty similar shape, and also sports those beloved Hall effect joysticks. It does have a little bit of a mushy d-pad but hey, look at that lovely colourway!

Finally, if you're looking to spend as little as possible, the GameSir Nova Lite comes in as the cheapest option at a mere $18. It's got less mappable buttons than its successor thanks to no back paddles, and is overall a downgrade. For the extra four bucks I'd personally just go for the newer version, but if you're really looking to really squeeze every cent, it's certainly an option worth considering.

It's incredible to think you can spend so little and get a stick drift-resistant wireless controller that doesn't completely suck. Luckily for the GameSir Nova Lite, it does all of the above and manages to feel good and light in the hands, too.

Key specs: Wireless (Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz) | Asymmetric | Hall effect

#3782. Rockstar is actively shopping Red Dead Redemption movie and TV rights around, just don't expect the same for Grand Theft Auto

Rockstar Games is seemingly interested in expanding Red Dead Redemption beyond video games, after years of Hollywood knocking on its doors. According to a new report, the company is looking for someone to pick up the movie and TV rights for its open-world Westerner series.

The information comes from a new report in The Ankler, citing agents in the know. According to the report, Rockstar wanted something in the range of $100m (£76m) as a minimum for the license to its Red Dead Redemption series of games. As the report pointed out, Amazon paid $250m (£191m) in 2017 for Lord of the Rings' TV show rights alone.

Rockstar, however, is not interested in turning Grand Theft Auto into a movie or TV show, per the same report. It's not clear why the company is willing to entertain the idea for one franchise and not the other, but the vastly larger popularity of GTA (compared to RDR, at least) could explain why.

It's worth noting that streamers like Netflix and Amazon have been on something of a hot streak recently with the success of shows based on popular video games, such as Fallout. HBO managed to turn The Last of Us into a prestige series that can attract both fans of the game and casual TV viewers.

Indeed, many more video game-based shows are in the works, like Amazon's Tomb Raider series, its God of War adaptation, as well as FX's Far Cry anthology show. Even Call of Duty, a massive - though nowhere near as massive as GTA - franchise, is getting a live-action movie in 2028.

But none of those are as profitable or culturally-dominnant as Grand Theft Auto. GTA 6 just released, and immediately beat analyst expectations. The game made $3.79bn (£2.90bn) in revenue on day one off the back of 32.5m copies sold, making it the biggest launch of any entertainment product in history, so it's understandable why Rockstar is not too eager to turn it into a movie or TV show.

The wait for GTA 6 was undeniably long, with 13 years passing since Rockstar's last Grand Theft Auto entry dropped and its new behemoth – but fans aren't the only ones who felt the wait… those behind the game did, too.

Especially co-protagonist Lucia's own actor, Manni L. Perez, who says she's worked on Grand Theft Auto 6 for nearly ten years now – the majority of those 13 years following GTA 5. "Life has been such a whirlwind these past couple of days and I just want to take a moment to say thank you," she writes on Instagram. "Thank you to all the new followers, to all the beautiful messages, and the positive reception the game and my character have received."

She then recalls the amount of time she's spent in Lucia's shoes: "I've dedicated almost a decade to bringing Lucia to life. She's been such a significant part of mine and I am beyond grateful she now gets to be a small part of yours." That's one heck of a role, then, considering the amount of work Perez has evidently poured into it – and I'd say it's more than paid off. As it stands, GTA 6 continues to smash records as the highest-rated game of all time.

It's also already proven "the biggest launch in PlayStation history" (with Sony reporting "more than 39 million unique players" playing on just the PS5). Phew. Jason's own actor, Dylan Rourke, has posted on his profile as well, seemingly celebrating his time with Rockstar. "Thankful for this wild ride," Rourke's story reads. "Gratitude won't cut it. Make today about the ones you love. Family."

Wild ride, indeed… and I'd say it's far from over. The community is still eagerly awaiting a PC release (and no, I'm not talking about the unofficial ports in progress), and, of course, the hotly anticipated Online counterpart. Rockstar has yet to announce either, though, but both are sure to propel GTA 6 further into relentless popularity – if you can fathom it becoming any bigger than it is now.

#3780. Capcom dinosaur shooter Exoprimal's servers will go extinct next year, as shutdown meteor looms

Exoprimal, Capcom's 2023 team shooter pitting exosuited fighters against T-rexes, is the latest game to be handed an expiration date. Its online services will cease as of late September 2027, rendering it unplayable, with the game set to be delisted from stores in March.

Capcom announced as much in a post running through all of the permutations of the shutdown, which is coming on September 29th 2027 at 8AM PDT. "We cannot thank you enough for the love and support you have shown over the years, and we sincerely apologize for the gravity of this announcement," they wrote.

The publishers have already stopped selling Exoprimal's seasonal survival passes, with plans to pull the game itself and all DLC from sale as of March 30th 2027. Those who already own Exoprimal will be able to re-download it in the time between it being pulled from stores and the server shutdown in September, meaning there's plenty of time to hop in for a final few rounds of dino shooting if you fancy.

It's long seemed like only a matter of time before the dino shooter was taken offline, with Capcom having stopped releasing new seasonal additions to it all the way back in July 2024. So, this seems more like a natiral petering out than an instance of an online game being cut down in its prime or not long after launch, as we've seen recently with extreme cases like Highguard. As such, one would hope there's a chance plenty of Exoprimal devs have already been redirected onto other Capcom games, minimising the amount who might be left in the often precarious position of having nothing immediate to work on following this shutdown.

It's fair to say Ed Thorn (RPS in peace) wasn't a fan of Exoprimal on reviewing it at launch. "I thought Exoprimal somehow managed to make dinosaurs versus mechs, aka the coolest concept ever, boring in my review-in-progress,"he wrote. "I held out hope it would improve, though, as lots of commenters assured me it's fun side would finally surface. "Just play several more hours and things really open up! Variety in the dinos, in the modes, in just about everything!". To some extent, they were right. There are fun moments to be had as you queue up for Dino Survival and suddenly, remarkably, things have changed a bit.

"But the game doesn't respect your time. It forces you to sit through hours of repetitive dino-slaying and then only offers you the chance, the chance to slay dinos in a way that isn't excruciatingly samey. Even as someone who finds the fun in mindless carnage, I'd much rather ditch my mech suit and let the dinosaurs run rampant. The dinosaurs don't deserve this."

That's not exactly as positive a eulogy as the one offered by Capcom, but not all games are destined to stick the landing and be universally beloved mega-hits, especially those wading into the live service maelstrom.

Grabbing a Truffade Thrax in GTA 6 isn't too hard, but if you want Andrew Node's supercharged version, the true fastest car around, you'll need to complete a little collectible hunt. Before you start, it's worth noting that this special Truffade Thrax costs 70k to register when you steal it, though you can also sell it to Randy for 20k (not that I would recommend this as it's a unique car).

The first step is scanning ten No Flusher toilet graffiti stamps around Vice Beach, the east portion of Vice City, with your WAiNK It app. Each symbol is basically a little blue toilet. After that, you'll have to head to a secret lockup, and then you're on for stealing the car.

This first one is southeast of Nola - Ocean beach on the pavement on the west side of the road.

The second is east of Podium Sports - Ocean Beach, on the south side pavement of the road leading out onto the grass towards the beach.

This one is at the east end of the bridge leading from Vice Beach to Waxman Island, on the southern pavement. Also to the west of LTD Gas - Ocean Beach

This fourth one is east of Aural Expert and north of Venus Fitness, on the pavement at the side of the junction.

This one is on the pavement directly in front of Banana Hole Main Bar, east down the road from the previous one above.

This sixth one is on the sidewalk on the far west of the road running along the bottom of the huge park in Vice Beach.

This seventh is west of Podium Sports - Ocean Beach, down the road you can see with the roundabout at the end on the map.

The eighth is east down the road from Shorefront - Ocean Beach bank and south of Easy Electronics, on the pavement on the corner.

This ninth is north of Marshal's jewelry and northeast of Endzone - Washington Beach, at the east end of the big carpark bordering the beach.

On the right side of the northern road at the Oldby Island junction, directly opposite Ron Gas - Washington Beach.

After you've found all ten, Cal's conspiracy theory chat (which unlocks after the first) will go dark, before you get a separate message a little later giving you their hideout location. Head there, read the note to the right of the garage door, and then look on the back of it to get the code for the lock:

Inside you'll have a bunch of evidence pointing to Andrew Node's house on Starfish island, so examine it all and then you're ready to steal the car.

First off, Starfish Island is a gated community with security, so it's better to get a boat there. Head west from the hideout and steal a boat on the piers, then drive west across the water to the jetty of Andrew Node's house—it's the one on the southern side towards the centre, that looks like a backwards L.

Dock, head around the left side of the house to find a white garage on the right you can open up with Andrew Node's Truffade Thrax inside. You'll have to drive it off the island, but after that you can head to Randy and register it for 70k. Just make sure you have the garage space and the money before you steal the car.

#3777. Unofficial GTA 6 PC port effort suffers setback as Rockstar seemingly takes down Project Leonida, one of the internet's biggest recompilation projects

A lot has happened in the last 24 hours in the community working to get Grand Theft Auto 6 running on PC. And now, Rockstar has dealt a major blow to their efforts.

After infamous leaker CyberLeek made good on their promise and released a full Xbox build of GTA 6, the build immediately spread online amongst modders and recompilers. Their goal? Get the game playable on PC as soon as possible.

The largest hub of all that activity has been the Project Leonida Discord server, which had its own repository and a team of volunteer modders working - with help from Claude AI - to recompile GTA 6's leaked Xbox build to run on PC. Rockstar has allegedly taken down the server, causing the project's leaders to dismantle the entire operation.

Project Leonida's lead NotRexed posted on X to announce they're ending development, after fans noticed the Discord server has been removed, as has Project Leonida's GitHub repository.

"I quit guys. I'm sorry," NotRexed wrote. "I really want to make cool stuff but every single time shit happens that I can't control so I'm stepping away. Thank you everybody, especially in the discord that allowed me to have this opportunity."

The modder, who claims to be a "15 year-old kid", later wrote in a follow-up X post that Rockstar is behind the server's takedown, though that's not the only reason for the project's end.

"Last post from me. I wanna clear things up," they wrote. "Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I've said before, I'm a 15 year-old kid. Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye."

Before the Project Leonida server disappeared, footage emerged showing GTA 6 running on PC. The game is able to reach the initial setup screen, but quickly goes into a black screen afterwards. As unimpressive as the result was, it was achieved within hours of the full Xbox build's leak.

Incidentally, while Project Leonida was the biggest and most prominent of the various GTA 6 recompilation projects, the leaking of the full Xbox build has given rise to various other groups. PortWatch VI is a website dedicated to tracking their progress, and though the data is almost entirely self-reported, a few other teams appear to have made notable progress themselves, so this may not be the end of the story.

Rockstar has yet to comment publicly on the Xbox build's leak, and the company has not announced GTA 6 for PC. However, a report suggested GTA 6 arrives on PC in the first quarter of 2027, earlier than everyone expected.

We haven't heard much about the Iron Man game at EA's Motive Studio since it was announced in 2022. Really, we haven't heard anything, but there's been a reasonable suggestion that we'll finally learn more at this year's The Game Awards.

The first and most prominent clue that something is brewing comes from the company itself, as the official website's been revamped. There's no mention of Iron Man anywhere on the site, but the fact it's been made to look all nice and sleek indicates someone's taking care of it, and there may well be a flurry of activity on the way.

On top of that, you have The Game Awards itself being sponsored by Disney this year. The ceremony is being livestreamed on Disney Plus, and a significant number of projects under the House of Mouse are expected to appear.

Marvel Studios has been part of the Disney stable for years now. That includes the billionaire philanthropist Tony Stark and his exploits as Iron Man. A purported trailer actually leaked back in August for this release, just showing Tony putting on the suit. It's rough and clearly a work-in-progress - but that could be because it's being tinkered with for a certain worldwide showcase.

Throw in the synergy of The Game Awards occurring right before Avengers: Doomsday arrives in cinemas, featuring a returning Robert Downey Jr. as the eponymous villain Doctor Doom, and it all lines up, really. The timing is conspicuous, even if it doesn't indicate much other than that.

I would expect a few Marvel-related games across the show regardless. The MCU is headed into another era with Doomsday and the follow-up, Avengers: Secret Wars, and that includes finally bringing the X-Men back to the big screen.

Arkane's Blade and Plaion's Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra are good candidates for turning up as well, though Blade remains mired in Microsoft's ongoing layoff wave. After that, who knows? Maybe the fabled Black Panther solo game will appear and we might get the first details on Spider-Man 3. All are exciting prospects, but should he make an appearance, expect Tony to steal the show.

#3774. Inside Retro Reset, the "really inspirational" father and son project teaching kids about classic games hardware from aboard a converted bus

"When they have written some code, nearly all of them have a big smile on their face"

At first the kids jostle to get to the games that they know. "Welcome to the Retro Reset Bus," says Luke Stoner as the students push to get to the screen that’s caught their eye. Sonic on the Sega Mega Drive is the first they see, and the quickest student to get on board the bus looks triumphant as he nabs the stool in front of the console. Jason, Luke’s dad, asks him what he thinks about the graphics – slightly grainy and slightly pixelated – but he’s not at all bothered and soon engrossed. After a few minutes, though, his eyes keep moving to the back of the bus where "Jackson is a wally" is now emblazoned across a flickering screen in seven different colours. Jackson then gives out a chuffed yell when his code finally works after a couple of restarts. His retort to his mate appears on the 1981 BBC Micro Model B‘s screen as the other students crane to have a look. This is, incidentally, the machine that turned a national broadcaster into a computer retailer (with help from Acorn), says Jason.

Luke’s knowledge is beautiful but the students also find him approachable. As Jason shares: "It’s really inspirational for kids coming onto a bus that they can talk to someone younger like Luke, who knows his stuff and has made something incredible happen." One student asks where Minecraft is and Luke explains that it doesn’t fit the parameter of being more than twenty years old yet, sharing details of when it was published and by who. Roblox could be included, but Luke isn’t keen because of recent controversies around safety. When this group are reluctantly herded off the bus by even more reluctant teachers, another heads in with just a little gap for resetting the machines and cramming a biscuit.

The bleeps and blips start from the machines as the students start playing. One teacher stops at the Atari 2600 and shares that her family has just bought her one. She is loving the daily dose of nostalgia. Luke and Jason move up and down the bus answering questions, resetting machines and showing the students their collection of old phones. One student winces at he is passed the bag that would have carried the battery for a Panasonic EB-3600 "brick" phone from 1989. When Jason says his dad had one, they give that look of pity reserved for anyone over 30 but are also incredulous that anyone would lug that around, especially when the phone could only do calls. When Jason asks if anyone would like to break an iPhone and have a look inside, all of the hands shoot up. He then talks about memory, RAM and chips, brings out a floppy disk; and tells the tale of where the expression "computer bug" came from. Still, it's the game on a tape - Jungle Story for the Commodore 64 - which they all turn away from screens to see. Perhaps we have Stranger Things to thank, but the tape has retro currency and they all think it’s sick.

The event is being run by East Sussex Careers Hub and is specifically aimed at students with SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities). More than twenty-five schools turn up and most teachers leave with a flyer, chatting to colleagues about where the bus could park onsite. Jason says that the response to the bus, since Retro Reset's launch as a registered charity in August 2025, has been phenomenal, and they could easily fill a full week with visits. For now, he is juggling it with work commitments.

The bus was Luke’s idea and inspired by a visit to The Centre for Computing History in Cambridge, where visitors can get their hands on home computers and consoles from decades gone by. The family started thinking about what was possible and finally, after Luke finished college, began kitting out the bus: buying or accepting donations of hardware, researching which monitors would work with the ancient systems, and installing it all within the cabin.

On a basic level, the charity is telling the story of how technology has iterated. But by allowing visitors to take apart their machines, and giving brief lessons in coding with Basic, it also pulls the veil back on the work that goes into making a game - while opening students' eyes to what they could create themselves. "I guess it’s bridging the gap between the polished and finished latest game," Jason says, "which could be perceived as not achievable for them, to seeing how all that coding came about. Other than making sure they are really accurate with their typing; they realise that coding can be quite simple and something that they can actually do. I would go further and say that when they have written some code, nearly all of them have a big smile on their face." This, he hopes, might be the spark for some students to get into coding, especially for PC games, where under-18s are an underrepresented demographic.

It also hit the road as the popularity of retro gaming continued to surge. According to a Consumer Reports survey published last February, 14% of US gamers regularly play games made before 2000. This is reflected in the staggering stat that the retro gaming market is estimated to be worth $3.8 billion globally, with a projected rise to $8 billion by 2033. Retro-focused videos on YouTube and TikTok rack up millions of views of views, and communities formed on reddit or Discord - some with hundreds of thousands of members - discuss nothing else.

Nostalgia is playing a huge part. Atari’s Implicit Conversations is built on just this, creating retro games for modern consoles like PlayStation 5 or the Nintendo Switch. For Luke, though, this misses the point. He likes the click when you put a cartridge in a machine; and he likes that he is just him and the game. The parents of visiting students appreciate this too, and often share how overwhelming it feels to keep their kids safe in the online gaming environment. "Parents of younger children [tell us that] they hate that Minecraft and Roblox can allow their kids to play against perceived strangers. Even the more technical parents say they still miss safety measures and would prefer the games not be online at all," Jason explains.

Last month, Ofcom published its Growing Up Gaming summary report, which found that almost two-thirds (64%) of parents of three to 17 year olds who game online are concerned about their child talking to strangers through games or their chat functions. And, while the vast majority of young players go online without incident, it is true that those who use chat functions will likely interact with strangers. The same research found that more than half (55%) of children who game online say they play with people they have never met offline at least sometimes, while one in five (20%) do so all or most of the time they play.

By contrast, Jason claims that not one student has asked if they can get online, and he’s also never seen one get out their phone when they’re on the bus. Perhaps it is a welcomed break. "We offer a completely safe environment to come and experience these games and machines. That's really what we're here for," he states.

Luke shares too that he became nervous of the data he was sharing with gaming companies, and conscious that this was all being stored, thus making it vulnerable to breaches. He also baulked at what he felt was a constant money grab from gaming companies, including moves that render games unsupported or completely obsolete. Retro gaming is cheap in comparison and therefore more accessible, especially for younger players. "When you tell them that they can get an old console for less than £100 and often games come free when you buy them second hand, their ears really prick up," Jason says. "For a lot of the youngsters, the cost of modern gaming equipment is unattainable. And of course, we explain that they could take old computers and laptops and then load free operating software onto them. This gets them online, often for free. Once they are there, they can game."

John W. Champeau is founder of Champ Games, a Connecticut-based venture, which develops retro games system primarily for the Atari 2600. He has Scramble, Galagon, Gorf Arcade and Elevator Agent on his line-up. He agrees that price point is a huge part of the appeal of retro gaming. "Atari has released a line of "+" systems that are modern reinterpretations of the class Atari 2600 and 7800 hardware, but at a lower price point but with modern conveniences such as HDMI support, firmware updates, and new controllers," he notes. These systems can also play older cartridges that were released back in the day. "This means that the games themselves can be acquired at a low cost as well, sometimes even free if someone is lucky enough to know someone with a box of old Atari carts in their basement or attic."

But there may also be something intrinsically different about how these games are designed to be played that is driving their renaissance. In December 2025, Newsweek shared the views of two mental health professionals that "90s Video Games Were Better for Kids’ Brains." In what was sure to be a contentious piece (and perhaps that was the point), mental health counsellor Veronica Lichtenstein, and Melissa Gallagher, a licensed clinical social worker, argued that the very nature of gaming has changed and is now damaging. Retro games had a start and an end – and with the latter came a big hit of dopamine for achieving victory. Modern games are designed as "loops for addiction" with no real end; and constant prompts to buy. Satisfaction is constantly deferred. Lichtenstein also says that modern games leave little room for critical thinking, as a quick search online will delivers solutions if a player ever gets stuck.

Champeau agrees. "Our games are not designed to be addictive 'time stealers' like some modern video games that encourage players to 'stay online' for hours on end to acquire additional resources needed to complete a game or advance to a new level, etc," he says, adding: "All of our games are designed to be short burst distractions that don't rely on long gaming sessions to feel a sense of accomplishment.” He says that the lower graphics resolution and primitive sounds are actually a relief for many after years of hyper-realistic gaming. "Retro games distance the gap between game and reality, which was the intention of video games in the first place," he argues.

Back on the bus, Sonic may have attracted the initial crowds but it is now Pacman and the Binatone that the students are huddling around. Jason has given up one control for the tennis game to a student and a noisy competition is now taking place. The graphics are basic as is the premise, but scoring is tricky and the battle to get to 15 points hard-fought. The teacher laughs. "The bleeps from that game are bringing back memories," she says as she tries to encourage her students to finish and hand over the controllers. But with faces lit up by the screen and set in concentration, they don’t hear her. This is play for play’s sake, with no distractions, and could be why the games of the past might be just the future these kids need.

#3773. Today's Nintendo Switch Online update finally introduces a feature players have been asking for since 2018

There's been an exciting addition to the Nintendo Classics GameCube app today, as users have discovered a small - but oft-requested - change in the software's Version 2.2.0.

This new option arrived fairly quietly as part of an update that otherwise introduced Wave Race: Blue Storm to the Nintendo Classics – GameCube lineup. That addition may have generated the most headlines, but it's this one little toggle that's getting many players exicted.

Why is this such a big deal? Previously, the bordered image on the 4:3 aspect ratio games contained lots of little dots, and players complained that these were distracting at best, and casused discomfort on the eyes whilst playing at worst. Other players worried it would contribute to screen burn-in on older televsion sets. As part of the new update, you can simply border your games with plain black - a tiny revision, but one that you can already see online communities celebrating. The player icon (another UI element that attracts derision) is still present, however, but as one comment summarises: "it's a step in the right direction".

"Oh my gawd, I've been wanting this! I hate the checkered on the side, it clashed with every game I tried," says one social media user." Players have been complaining about these borders and UI elements since Nintendo Classics was introduced on the Nintendo Switch back on 18th September, 2018. So it's taken a good eight years for Nintendo to - finally - implement a change.

In order to change the border yourself, you need to head to the game library selection screen on the Nintendo Classics app, navigate to the game settings, and locate the option to toggle this border graphic in the "Extra Elements Display" tab. Hit the button and - bang - you're done. At the time of writing, this option only appears on the GameCue app, and only on Switch 2, but people on social media are already asking Nintendo to enable it across the original Switch and other apps in the library, too.

Not everyone is happy with the 'slowly, slowly' approach Nintendo is taking towards implementing these changes, though. "Why can't we expect the full step with no graphic at all?" asks one irritated poster on Reddit. "Why do you have to deal with these half assed implementations for a paid deluxe subscription service?"

"Oh well, probably gotta wait another 10 years for the next improvement" says another. Another slightly more constructive user outlines what helpful additons might look like, noting that adding a "blurred zoomed in image of the game to fill out the background, or just extending the colors outward into the border, or maybe something fun like a CRT TV-looking border like the NES and SNES Classic had" would go a long way to make the retro experience better on the consoles.

The Bravado Banshee is another one of the cars you'll need to track down for Randy in GTA 6, but unlike the Pegassi Infernus, this one doesn't involve anything as dodgy as robbing a police lockup.

You can find this car inside the Sunrise Premium Autos showroom at the north tip of Southside, southwest of Pay 'N' Spray - Salton or east across the road from Ron Gas - Southside. This region is to the northeast of Hamlet.

There are two showrooms here, so make sure you have the right one, though the other does contain Pfister Growlers, in case you haven't gotten that car for Randy yet, either. Head inside to find the car—if you've played previous GTAs, you'll recognise it as a convertible with a white stripe down the middle. Hop inside, use the key cloner, and drive it through the glass.

This might damage it a bit, but you can always repair it at Ron Gas nearby, or at the gas station near Randy's shop. Just remember to drive fast, and if the tracker starts to beep, speed up to stop it pinging your location to the cops. Delivering this one gets you 6,500k and a 5k condition bonus as usual if it's in good nick.

#3771. Any official GTA 6 PC port’s ability to deliver a proper first person mode would be its biggest ace in the hole, so reckon I, a traitor

GTA 5 and Red Dead 2 both got ‘em, but Rockstar’s latest offering feels their most first person-coded yet

To be fair, I’ve made no secret of my plans to do just that if you’ve read any of our recent roundups of what everyone’s playing over the weekend. I can understand why it might leave a sour taste in the mouth, but it is what it is. No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the big game of the moment is forced into my hands.

Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points. You know, better graphics, superior performance, and modding. Historically, Rockstar’s crime sandboxes are games played from the third person perspective. That shot lingering behind Niko Bellic as he jogs around Brooklyn with a rocket launcher or following the damn bike of CJ as he in turn follows that damn train. This is the default way GTA’s breakneck action is presented to the player and was with GTA 5 at launch.

As Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into. In order to do that, while simultaneously pushing the detail and graphical boundaries of their rendered worlds, Rockstar have needed to squeeze every bit of juice they can from the available hardware. Red Dead Redemption 2 managed to include a full first person mode at launch. GTA 6 hasn’t been so lucky, even if there are moments when bringing up your phone or reading a note temporarily lodges the camera into Jason and Lucia’s noggins.

There is a way to glitch yourself into a more permanent first person perspective, but it’s naturally not got the polish that a proper first person mode would. What it does do is make clear that, with vehicle interiors lavishly detailed and some gun animations looking natural rather than janky, any port using the PC's extra horses to deliver a proper first person mode seems a no brainer, if not something already set in stone.

Assuming that is the case, I frankly can’t see why first person won’t become the go-to perspective on PC. Even more so than RDR2, GTA 6 feels like a game built to belong in first person. It dedicates so much time and energy to engaging you in every aspect of Jason and Lucia’s routines, rendering everything from eating to working out to doing up a house (and the acts involved in doing a robbery, I guess) in such exhaustive detail and depth that it’s almost beyond parody.

Notifications ping about you needing to finish a bench pressing session where every rep involves holding and releasing R2 and L2 at just the right time. An app tells you you’re hungry, so you wander over to the fridge, pick out a protein shake to down, then press R2 to lob the bottle in the bin, assuming you’re keen to keep your flat tidy. Shopping trips see you pick up groceries off shelves, stow them in a bag, then run home with it tucked under your arm because you’ve brought a motorbike and forgotten it lacks a boot. Every stickup begins with the ritual of picking your longarm gun out of your car’s boot, where it might have sat next to a bag of drugs you’ve stowed to deliver to a fence later. Stopping off to switch cars and clothes to throw the cops off your scent is no longer just for overenthusiastic roleplayers.

The fact that the game goes to such lengths only to maintain the detachment inherent to the third person view feels bizarrely antithetical at times, like an exhibition of a tiny Fabergé egg that you’re forced to view through a telescope from the surface of Mars. The massive efforts of Rockstar’s developers - many of whom are currently trying to gain formal union recognition or have been fighting the company at an employment tribunal over firings they argue were unjust - went into putting together an artwork that regularly ends up at an arm’s length out of necessity, despite packing intricacies likely best seen through a magnifying glass.

Enter the PC release. And possibly nothing else offering the same bang for your buck around the same time. With GTA 5, the PS4 and Xbox One got an enhanced version of the game around the time of the PC port, offering a number of extra features - including a first person mode. Rockstar were quick to rule out GTA 6 getting 60 or 40fps performance modes on current console hardware due to a lack of horses, and if that also applies to a first person mode, then such a thing might only come with the next generation of consoles. That’d be the PS6 and Xbox’s Project Helix, neither of which seem hugely imminent and could well end up boasting ludicrous prices thanks to the ongoing memory shortages.

So, those who already own a PC capable of running any GTA 6 port could be in the best position to enjoy the game from a Jason and Lucia-eye view the moment such a thing becomes possible. Sure, it would also look and run better, but to be brutally honest I’ve found it looks damn gorgeous and runs acceptably on PS5. Sure, modding will no doubt spring up must-have additions, but the base game already works in plenty of the roleplaying mechanics and in-depth side-jobbing that a lot of popular GTA 5 mods delivered.

Thus, that window as the place to play GTA 6 as it feels intended, in first person, is what I’d currently peg as the best chance for the crimsim to be not just a great game you can play on PC - as I’d argue Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 are - but a great PC game that’s inarguably best experienced on our platform of choice. I don’t think writing that is falling into the trap it’s easy to end up in with big games that hit console first: declaring in salesman-like fashion that they’ll of course be better on PC by default, in a manner that sometimes feels a bit like you’re trying to convince yourself that you’ve not paid more than a pre-RAM crisis console buyer for nothing.

I’d never consider playing Cyberpunk 2077 in anything but first person on PC. GTA 6, from what I’ve played thus far, could be the next uber-detailed open world I spend hundreds of hours taking in the sights of, ideally through the eyes of a highly dangerous and highly stylish operator on the prowl for lucrative underworld opportunities.
