Blizzard's latest patch prevents Alterac Valley from being a glorified reputation farm.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite being set in the past, WoW: Forever is an attempt to capture the spirit of the old game by injecting it with new quirks that challenge new and returning players alike to approach it differently than any other version of the MMO. This is why familiar old dungeons can drop new loot, like an armor set that turns you into a snake.

Blizzard has said that its goal is to "unsolve" the game as best it can so players don't settle into the same routines they're used to. This is especially true for min-maxed strategies that threaten to suck the fun out of enjoying the game, or "the journey", as Blizzard likes to call it.

It's a lofty goal that can't be achieved without persistently fiddling with the knobs that encourage players to do one thing over another—which is the very thing that differentiates WoW: Forever from WoW Classic.

This week, Blizzard stepped in to fix a problem that was brewing in its 40-player MOBA-esque PvP mode Alterac Valley. Players were avoiding PvP altogether, turning it into a glorified reputation farm.

"We’ve seen that players in Alterac Valley were frequently completing the battleground without capturing the objectives, so we’ve made some adjustments to incentivize a focus on the objectives rather than rushing to kill the enemy faction’s general," community manager Kaivax wrote.

The patch basically broke a popular 'zerg' strategy where one side rushed to end the match as fast as possible by beefing up the NPC defenders that stood in their way. Blizzard shifted some of the reputation and honor you'd normally get from killing the generals to the other objectives so players are encouraged to engage with the whole mode.

But, as I've seen with changes like this in the past few weeks, many players are upset that they can't just spam it for the rewards, and that others have already reaped the benefits of the old strategy. There are people in Reddit threads doing the math to highlight how much efficiency has been lost (it doesn't seem like much) and questioning the point of doing Alterac Valley at all.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While I sympathize with not wanting to do something that feels like a chore, it's a far worse problem to have an entire part of the game flattened into an AFK farm. Alterac Valley is supposed to feel like a large-scale war where you look at a big map and choose what objectives are worth fighting over as you try to weaken the enemy forces. The loot you get from maxing out your reputation with the associated factions is meant to be a reward for putting in the effort to learn what it takes to win.

The whole pitch for WoW: Forever is that it's not going to ditch everything with a new expansion every few years. Numbers can be tweaked down the line if the reputation grind is too much of a slog, but the mode should be fun to play so it's not treated like a box to check off in your character's journey. An inert PvP mode ruins the spirit of the MMO far more than a slightly longer reputation grind does.

I think this is a good example of a healthy change that shows Blizzard is committed to protecting core parts of the experience from becoming a treadmill that nobody enjoys. WoW: Forever's strengths are the ways it encourages you to participate in systems that aren't there to fill progression bars. As Harvey said in his WoW: Forever review, "Forever is proof that old-school MMO design deserves a second chance," and that requires taking a stance on what the game is and isn't meant to be.

#3719. "Does changing where games run cross a legal line?" Microsoft-owned Github ask in now-deleted post celebrating GTA 6's effect on PC port-focused PS5 emulator

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on GitHub"

'Yay, GTA 6 is out on consoles and lots of people are playing it' is a fairly harmless thing to say. Unless you're, I dunno, a development platform mentioning that in a post celebrating the recent success of a PS5 emulator used for making unofficial PC ports of console games. You know, the sorts of unofficial PC ports vibecoders and proper coders having been scrambling to make of GTA 6 since its Xbox executable was allegedly leaked. The sorts of unofficial PC ports publishers like Rockstar tend to quickly move to have taken down.

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," read a Github tweet screengabbed by Kotaku before it was deep sixed. "The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line? Share your take. Happy GTA VImas!"

A video alongside the post seems to have dug the hole even deeper. "The project rewrites a game's executable so Windows and Linux can run it directly," a presenter cheerily declared. "Performance seems to be the main issue for users wanting to run GTA 6, with one contributor telling the project's community to lock in and get their agents to help if they need to." From there, the "big question" of whether it's actually legal to change where and how your games run was posed by Github.

And now their tweet is deleted. Here was the text. https://t.co/kNbmmPCGdf

One can only imagine how raised the eyebrows of Rockstar affiliated lawyers may have become if they read the post before Github yanked it.

Another big question posed a lot recently is whether the threat of bodged PC recreations based on the alleged leaked executable may lead Rockstar to narrow the gap between GTA 6's console release and its eventual Windows launch, which reports have previously claimed is planned for the opening months of next year. You know, because the company and publishers Take-Two presumably don't want to risk the sales of an official port being undercut by an unofficial one, no matter the degree of impact that might actually have (my presumption would be the official port would still rake in a fortune).

Given the reception their baffling AnyPS5 post received, I doubt Github'll be providing any more commentary on the rush to unofficially port GTA 6 and the debate as to when it might hit PC officially.

#3718. Blizzard is making a lot of the Diablo 4's event-specific Diablo 2 anniversary content permanent because everyone loved it in Season 15

Blizzard has officially unveiled Diablo 4's next live-service season: Season of Tyrael's Gambit. This is the ARPG's 16th season, and it follows on from the popular and well-received Season of Hell's Legacy.

In an unexpected move, Blizzard announced it's keeping some of the nostalgia-laiden content from the previous season, Season of Hell's Legacy, as a permanent addition. This is unusual, as the ephemeral nature of live seasons means new content goes away at the end of each season.

Season of Hell's Legacy paid tribute to Diablo's legacy and its 30th anniversary by introducing a lot of content inspired by previous Diablo games, chiefly Diablo 2. The list includes the return of iconic character Deckard Cain, a recreation of Old Tristram, and a big fight against the three Prime Evils - Diablo, Baal, and Mephisto - in their classic forms.

"We heard overwhelming requests for features from Season of Hell's Legacy to carry forward as permanent game features," Blizzard wrote in Season 16's announcement post. "While the entire season couldn't come along for the ride, we are implementing the following features with the launch of Season of Tyrael's Gambit that will carry forward in both Eternal and Seasonal realms."

Season of Tyrael's Gambit kicks off 1st December, so you still have time to access all of that in Diablo 4 until Season 15 ends. Certain things, such as craftable items, won't return, so you may as well try them while you can. That said, Blizzard is aware of the love some of those items have, and the developer said it may bring them back in the future.

Ariana Grande stepped away from the public after discourse about her appearance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ariana Grande is a wildly popular pop star and Oscar-nominated actress who has spent much of her life in the public eye. Over the past few years there's been a ton of discourse about her relationship with Cynthia Erivo while promoting the Wicked movies, as well as discourse about her appearance. The chatter got so loud that Grande took a step away from the public, although she recently reunited with Bowen Yang and talked about the backlash to her "Petal" music video.

Over the years Ariana Grande has spoken about her complicated relationship with the public, including discourse about her appearance and acting abilities. Those topics were addressed in her music video for "Petal", and during a recent appearance on the podcast Las Culturistas (which is streaming with a Hulu subscription) the accomplished multihyphenate spoke about the story she was telling in that video, offering:

That was largely what the video was about is like 'Oh, here comes this little girl, talented little girl.' And there's always some distortion around the performance or around the art, whatever it is. And for a while she tries to... and then my favorite part is that she comes back to herself at the end. She's wearing the same color, she's wearing the same hair, she's wearing the same thing. And that's when they say they say to her 'It's just so weird, go back to your old you.' And she's like 'But I am! I've connected with my inner me. This is me trying again as me.'

Grande addressed the "distortion" between her self-image and fan discourse throughout the entire album Petal, especially the title track. Clearly the 33 year-old singer saw the comments online, and backlash related to a change in her sound, the years-long Wicked promotional tour, as well as her personal appearance. Unfortunately, the "Petal" video inspired a new round of discourse that seemingly informed her decision to take some time away.

Shortly after the "Petal" video arrived online months ago, critics started commenting about her appearance, specifically her weight. This discourse started during Wicked, and continued despite Grande trying to address the chatter through her art. As she went on to share with Las Culturistas hosts Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers:

Then that video with the intention of really spelling it out had its own meta insane perception that was just really interesting. But I feel so proud and grateful. I wouldn't change a thing. I would put it out today exactly as is. I wouldn't change a thing. I think my experience of putting art out and having people receive it is so different than how it used to be, even just a few years ago.

Fame is a double edged sword, and most of us would likely crack under the pressure of this backlash. Ariana Grande set some boundaries to care for her mental health, but she also seemingly stands by her artistic choices related to the "Petal" music video. She went on to explain her perspective about the outside voices, saying:

And now I really do feel as long as I'm creating from an authentic place, and being honest, and sharing what I know needs to come out and making things that I love I know. Let the chips fall where they may. My people will be my people. And it's okay if they're not.

That certainly sounds like a healthy way to approach any potential backlash that Ariana Grande faces moving forward. She's once again putting herself out there with her starring role in Focker In-Law, as well as the recently announced documentary The Eternal Sunshine Diaries (the latter of which is arriving for those with a Paramount+ subscription). Hopefully expressing herself honestly in both that doc and podcast appearances like Las Cultch can help quiet the chatter from naysayers who are constantly weighing in about her career, personal life, and appearance.

Focker In-Law is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list, while the two-part The Eternal Sunshine doc will arrive on Paramount+ December 11th and 12th.

#3716. Drone Pilots have come to Cyber Knights: Flashpoint, the stealth tactics game's "most complex" class yet, alongside a pet system and the promise of "assassin cats"

How dare you accuse me of being a friendless loser! I have loads of friends! Their names are R2-D2 and Clippy and Arnold and Rosie the Maid. They all live in my rucksack, ready and waiting should I need somebody to dupe a security guard or fill the air around me with explosive chaff. All except Clippy, that is. He's too chonky to stuff in a bag, which can make for tricky mission extractions, but he compensates for that with his generous selection of *voice drops six octaves* FULLY LOADED AUTOCANNONS.

With friends like these, who needs human allies? It's time to play stealth tactics sim Cyber Knights: Flashpoint the way it was meant to be played: skulking in a hole while buzzing, clanking mechabastards cleanse the map of any and all defenders. Don't spare the lead, Rosie. You were not built to understand mercy.

Let's try that again: wireheady heist-me-do Cyber Knights: Flashpoint has received a major update adding a new player class, the Drone Pilot, billed by developers Trese Brothers as "the most complex" and among the most "flexible" of the game's Neuromantic vocations. The Drone Pilot arrives alongside a new pet system they'll be using down the road for "warhunds and assassin cats". Right now, though, the only "pets" at your disposal appear to be those drones. Here's what they're good for: "jamming enemy systems, disabling security devices in passing, hijacking enemy drones to turn on their own side, or trailing fields of shredding nano-chaff and squad-boosting support zones wherever the drone flies."

Drones come in three types, light (fast and best for stealthy support), medium (a mix of support and combat-oriented), and heavy (flying forts and/or stomping murder mechs). Light or medium drones are deployed from your backpack, and auto-extract when you do, no matter where they are. Heavy drones deploy alongside you at mission start, and have to be within nine metres of you when you extract, potentially trapping you on the map. Each drone chassis has its own weapon and armour setup, plus a choice of modules that grant Talents (abilities).

While rolling a Drone Pilot might seem like an opportunity to forgo any and all squidgy organic accomplices, the big catch is that Drone Pilots and their mecha mates share action and movement points. While using the Full Pilot talent, you can transfer AP to a drone so that it can move and fight like a full separate character. While using the Auto-Pilot talent, you'll only share bonus MP. There's also the option to multi-class, with Trese Brothers noting that "dipping into another class can significantly increase their flexibility or buff their personal abilities with just a few talents from an alternate tree".

As for how you'll get your hands on the Drone Pilot class, their costs make them a poor fit for teams with a power level below three, so they aren't among the New Game options. You'll be able to recruit them in the Underworld Hub and also, turn characters into drone pilots once you acquire a Pilot Wire cybernetic implant and the requisite cyber surgery. The Pilot Wire uses up a Deep Brain slot, making the class incompatible with the Hacker or Wireghost classes. Beyond that, you can reach out to a smuggler or broker to get access to new and better drones and pilot cybernetics.

Pettable killdroids aside, Trese Brothers are continuing work on Cyber Knight's mod support. The latest update adds features for official language translation mods and Attribute bonus tweaking, alongside expanded Legwork options. They're also labouring away on a modkit preview project of some kind. Read more on Steam.

New to Cyber Knights? Congratulations on digesting all the above gibberish about weaponised WALL-Es. I can only assume you read the whole thing in hopes of further talk of "assassin cats", but alas, Trese Brothers are maintaining an ominous silence. Instead, here is what Nic Reuben (RPS in peace) had to say about the game in our 2025 review: "Don't let its initial cyber-posturing and sheer amount of systems intimidate you. Cyber Knights: Flashpoint is wider than it is oppressively deep, while still being rich enough to offer up some excellently tense and entertaining stealth tactics."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Stranger Than Heaven is a notable departure for Yakuza and Like a Dragon developer RGG Studio, not least because it does away with the fast-paced, freewheeling combat of its previous brawlers in favor of a grittier, more grounded fighting system. The new combat has gotten a mixed response in early previews, but studio head and executive director Masayoshi Yokoyama believes challenging the status quo is key to being a great game developer.

When you fight in Stranger Than Heaven, the left and right sides of the controller correspond to the left and right sides of your body. The left bumper will throw out a quick left jab, while a pull of the right trigger will have protagonist Makoto Daito deliver a heavier bow from his right arm. Yokoyama explains this control scheme for Edge magazine in an exclusive Stranger Than Heaven cover story which you can read here on GamesRadar+.

“If you've never touched a controller before, you don't have any pre-established notions," Yokoyama explains, "so I think it's fairly common sense that if you hit the left button, you'd expect the left side of the character to move.” That kind of thinking, it seems, is part of Yokoyama's philosophy of game design.

"A slight diversion, but why are jeans blue?" he asks. "Nobody really thinks about this. But I think that people who ask these questions – people who doubt everything they see, and [wonder], 'Why is this the way it is?' – I have the conviction that those people are natural game creators."

Stranger Than Heaven's control philosophy reminds me a bit of the original Assassin's Creed, another game that rejected design conventions. There, the controller's face buttons correspond to different parts of the protagonist's body, with specific actions changing depending on context. Tapping the legs button, for example, might make you jump, dodge, or sprint.

Of course, the following Assassin's Creed games almost immediately abandon this puppeteering scheme in favor of more traditional controls, but the jury remains out on how Stranger Than Heaven's button mapping will feel through the full game. James loved the combat in September, but Josh wasn't a big fan of the fighting when he went hands-on with Stranger Than Heaven earlier this year. But perhaps there's another compelling argument to be made.

"We want to tell the story of Daito through our combat system," Yokoyama explained at the time. "When the game starts, Makoto is quite young and he's not a great fighter – this story takes you through 50 years of his life – in the same way that when the player starts the game, they won't be that skillful with the systems either. So we're hoping that by playing this character throughout the ages, the player themselves will grow alongside the character."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

To answer Yokoyama's rhetorical question, there are apparently an array of reasons that jeans are blue. The indigo they were historically dyed with was inexpensive, the color hid dirt, and it bonded durably with the denim threads. In other words, it solved multiple issues at once – I guess we'll find out if Stranger Than Heaven has found a similarly durable solution when it launches in January.

#3714. GTA 6 recompilers and vibe-coders implore AI chatbots to 'work faster' and 'make no mistakes' as they race to get the game running on PC

Things continue to get messy in the community of players working on getting Grand Theft Auto 6 working on PC. The previous frontrunner, Project Leonida, got their Discord server and GitHub repository taken down by Rockstar, but others have seemingly stepped in to finish the job.

The most up-to-date build of GTA 6 was allegedly leaked earlier this week by notorious leaker CyberLeek. This is a supposedly near-final build of the game's Xbox version, and it's seemingly being used as the basis for the recent work to port the game to PC.

Unsurprisingly, most of these communities of modders rely almost exclusively on generative-AI tools like Claude and Antigravity to decompile and recompile the console version of GTA 6. That has always been the case, but the CyberLeek build only invited even more to ask AI chatbots to make the PC port for them.

X user chasm has been following developments in the GTA 6 decompile and recompile communities, and recently shared some of the prompts the so-called vibe-coders are using - a few of whom livestreamed the process.

"Make no mistakes," one modder prompted the AI chatbot. "Keep finding more stuff and working and pushing," another eloquently asked. "Work faster," asked another. "There has to be a faster way to iterate than this," they continued.

Rockstar, which successfully managed to DMCA take down Project Leonida - including all of its 3,006 forks on lead author NotRexed's GitHub - is seemingly also going after people online discussing the community's progress. The X user in question later revealed they may no longer be able to share these updates, as their posts have also been removed "in response to a report by the copyright owner".

As for how far some of the remaining communities have managed to get, this video allegedly shows the game running on PC. This goes beyond the boot-up screen, which modders were able to reach within hours of CyberLeek's build alleged leaking.

The footage runs at sub-5fps, but the visuals look to have rendered normally. Assuming Rockstar doesn't also shut down the modders who remain active, we may see another progress update.

#3713. "A new era" for Vermintide 2 modding dawneth, as Fatshark release powerful new tools for custom levels, models and animations

Based on their own internal Stingray editing features

Pick up your feet, mayflies! Fatshark's co-op rat-whacker Warhammer: Vermintide 2 is getting some new mod tools. It already has a public SDK and modding framework, you say? Ah, but the new mod tools are better. They are a public-facing incarnation of the very same digital spellcraft Fatshark use to create the official levels and characters.

"While the Vermintide 2 Software Development Kit and the Vermintide Modding Framework have been out for years, these mostly only facilitated the development of purely code-related mods," the devs write on the official site. "There was no support for any other type of mod, and so creating mods that involved creating new assets has been either extremely difficult or impossible. But no more!

"The Mod Tools is a public release of our internal Stingray developer tools for Vermintide 2!" they continue. "This powerful set of tools will allow modders to work their magic on both editing and creating anything from custom levels, models, textures, particles, animations, and more! While it will probably take them a little while to cook exciting new mods, this marks a new era for Vermintide 2 modded content!"

OK, that's enough exclamation marks. The new mod tools are available to all owners of the game. You'll be able to find them in your Steam library, listed as "Modding Tools" and "Modding Tools content".

Fatshark have had to make a few "compromises" to get the new mod toolkit finished. "The weapon pack and the level that we mentioned in the past has been put on hold," the devs write. "We still want to get back to that, especially the weapon pack, but for now there is no active development on that. It’s important for us that we have transparency here, and while we are not working on these things, we do stick with our games! We have plans both near and far for Vermintide 2."

The Mod Tools rollout accompanies a change in server support. Hitherto, the Vermintide 2 modding scene has been split between the game's "Official Realm", where only officially sanctioned mods are allowed - "typically reserved for QoL mods that did not affect the experience much", the devs say – and the howling Chaos Wastes of the Modded Realm, which lets you install whatever grievous warpstone chicanery you please, at the cost of having no progression.

The lack of progression in Modded Realm has resulted in these servers "not seeing much use outside of niche communities", Fatshark claim. They're addressing that by, as you may guess, adding a Modded-only offline progression system, allowing players to scoop up loot and XP while performing weird experiments on the simulation.

Fatshark say they no longer have the capacity to keep up with mod approvals in the Official Realm, to say nothing of problems resulting from mods that have stopped receiving updates. They don't seem to have a solution for this, yet. They do, however, have a solution for an on-going lack of players in the dedicated Versus servers: shut down those servers! Let them crumple to dust!

"Versus is still playable, but it will be through community hosted games found through the Custom Game or the Lobby Browser," the devs assure. "This is already how most games of Versus are played, so we don’t think it will be a huge shake up in any shape or form, and it puts more of a focus on the Custom Game format where players have more control over the ruleset."

The shutdown will happen alongside the game's next update – Gifts of the Wolf Father, due in early December, which will rework the game's talent balance, update the weapon icons, and make the glow of different runes easier to distinguish from afar. Look out for more details down the line. In the meantime, please thrill my pointy ears with talk of Vermintide 2 mods. I've never touched that side of the game, and am wondering if there are any Skaven megaprojects I'm missing out on.

Microsoft-owned developer platform Github stepped in it earlier today when it posted a message on X celebrating the success of AnyPS5, an open source project that aims to let users port PS5 executables to PC, and then linked that success directly to efforts to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC. The message was deleted shortly after it was posted, but not before it was widely noticed and called out for being a very bad idea.

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," the message stated (via Kotaku).

"The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line? Share your take. Happy GTA VImas!"

Lest there be any misunderstanding, a video that accompanied the post made the GTA 6 connection explicit: "The project rewrites a game's executable so Windows and Linux can run it directly. Performance seems to be the main issue for users wanting to run GTA 6, with one contributor telling the project's community to 'lock in and get your agents to help' if they need to."

And here's the accompanying video from @github's GTA6 tweet https://t.co/crU9cpOWcsNovember 26, 2026

The question of whether or not this sort of thing crosses a legal line has, predictably, sparked debate among those who think they have a clear understanding of the answer. What caught most by surprise, though, is that Github—which is owned by Microsoft—would put forth the question in the first place, implicitly suggesting that it might not. GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive has been pretty aggressive with its efforts to keep recompiled versions of GTA 6 from landing on PC, and I can't imagine it would too thrilled with Github—which, I must emphasize, is owned by Microsoft—telling the world that it might actually be okay to go ahead and vibe-code it up.

That point wasn't missed by redditors, one of whom described it as Github "openly taunting Sony and Rockstar." Even the AnyPS5 subreddit seemed baffled: Redditor superkickstart asked, "Do they have AI running their socials? Lol"

There's also a little bit of irony in the fact that, until earlier this week, the leading effort to get GTA 6 running on PC was based on an Xbox build of the game posted by GTA 6 leaker Cyberleeks. Beyond that, there are also some very obvious questions about how Github (owned by Microsoft) would react to AI-powered ports of, say, other software:

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The whole thing is weird, really, because it seems like such an obviously bad idea. The only explanation I can come up with is that a social media manager either didn't think about it, didn't understand it (which would be weird in itself for someone doing social media posts for Github), or just had a big ol' brain fart. Whatever the reason, I imagine someone got a good old-fashioned talking-to about it.

I've reached out to Github and Take-Two for comment and will update if I receive a reply.

#3710. Keep the lighthouse on and the villagers obedient in Glagstone, an eerie island city-builder with Macintosh-style graphics

Now coming to Steam, following a Playdate prototype

Glagstone's "1-bit" aesthetic is a homage to Macintosh games of the late 1980s, cut with elements of art deco, Expressionism and film noir, but it looks like that mainly because it began life on lo-fi indie handheld Playdate.

In transplanting this eerie, story-driven city-builder to Steam, developers Valerii Krasnoselskii and Evgenii Kirichenko have fleshed out the tasty throwback art and shored up connections between the game's management and story layers, while leaving the crux of the experience untouched: you are the newly appointed governor of a remote northern island, contested by rival nations. You have come here to harvest the island's rich mineral resources, and now, the island is trying to drive you nuts.

You start by building homes and roads, getting fish to the warehouse, and churning out coal for the Crown. You'll also need to get the local lighthouse operational, so that you can see the city you're maintaining amid recurring fog, storms and darkness.

According to the devs, who've written a longer account of their project for 80.lv, it's supposed to feel like a simple sandbox, at first. But it has a creeping undertow. Visiting ships bring both opportunity and peril – admitting them to port is a gamble. The coastline is worryingly indefinite, in ways that can't quite be attributed to the tides. The locals are secretive, demanding and a little sinister. They talk of strange masked rituals, Silver Ladies, Shed Skins, and coves where you don't go during an eclipse. The Crown's orders, meanwhile, make less and less sense, and the waves keep coughing up peculiar objects. Sometimes, you could swear you hear singing through the surf.

A lot of the associated Dreadful Lore appears to arrive in the form of notebook marginalia, item descriptions, and sailor anecdotes that need to be coaxed forth with the promise of liquor. There are also pop-up events that may shape the morale and loyalty of your townsfolk. Those masked festivals, for example: they'll cost you production, but the glint in the village elder's eye suggests that refusing to give people time off for the Old Listening might be… reckless.

It all feels like an elaborate port fable from Failbetter's Sunless Sea. Or a standalone episode from fellow "1-bit" coastal sojourn World of Horror. You probably don't need me to tell you that Poe and Lovecraft are among the explicit influences. The developers – who are based in Belgrade and Basel - have also taken inspiration from the Svalbard and Novaya Zemlya archipelagoes. I've just googled Svalbard. It has very pretty reindeer. Haven't dug up any reports of kraken and mermaids just yet, but I'm sure they're out there.

Glagstone is coming to PC next year. Catch it on Steam - they're accepting playtest requests. Speaking as a fan of impenetrable marine murk, I think this looks wonderful. The 80.lv piece is worth reading through, however self-promotional - it includes some savoury titbits on how they've modelled the play of radiance between lighthouse beam and roadside lantern. Did you try the Playdate original? Any comments?

How Atlus' RPG quietly shaped CD Projekt Red's

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Persona 5 and Cyberpunk 2077, arguably the best RPGs ever made by Atlus and CD Projekt Red respectively, share some unexpected DNA, according to former Cyberpunk quest lead and now Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Paweł Sasko.

Sasko explained the JRPG's influence on CDPR's cyberpunk dystopia in a recent Twitter post in response to one user who examined how phone messages can be leveraged by a game's narrative. In the example this user shared, side character El César, whose money the player can choose not to take amid a fighting ring scandal, later tells the player that they've welcomed a new baby into his family. "Thanks for letting me go that time," he writes. "You've got a big heart for a merc."

This type of phone interaction was "inspired by some of the mechanics I saw in Persona 5 (and I really love this game)," says Sasko.

In Persona 5, released a few years before Cyberpunk 2077's 2020 launch (and quickly re-released as Persona 5 Royal in that same year), you regularly communicate with your friends via text message and group chat. This system is heavily used in the main story, and it also becomes important when managing Social Links, the character stories that power up your Personas and your party's abilities.

"It was an intuitive way to expand our narrative capabilities, while keeping the development costs pretty low," Sasko says of this phone correspondence. "Every time when all dialogs are written and sent to VO recordings we do add a substantial amount of texts, in the form of shards, emails, text messages, to build on the established narrative, flesh out consequences or add natural follow-ups.

"When done consistently across the whole game, it can really enrich the narrative. My favorite are all text exchanges with romance partners, some in a meaningful way contribute to character development."

Sasko has impeccable timing. GTA 6 has only just illustrated how meaningful and memorable in-game text messages can be. Developer Rockstar Games constructed a whole text and reminder system around protagonists Jason and Lucia, whose relationship is nurtured by all the little things in love that add up a lot, like a gift given for no reason, a thank you, an expression of concern, or a smiley photo.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

In GTA 6, a lot of this comes through in texts. The game will outright tell you that your partner will appreciate it if you do something specific. But more organically, interacting with them while they're halfway across the city really does add to the experience, to say nothing of many, many side characters, missions, and jobs to check on.

An intuitive phone interface can be very valuable for stories where phones make sense, not just because they allow for narrative snacks like an update from El César, but because they can help overlay our behavior – as we all walk around with unprecedented access to garbage-behind-a-screen in our pockets – with the character's, whether they're a student balancing school work with supernatural crises of the superego or a merc with a heart of gold.

Cyberpunk 2 is "making good progress," and CD Projekt is making sure fans don't have to wait so long between its RPGs in the future

Austin has been a game journalist for 12 years, having freelanced for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, IGN, Sports Illustrated, and more while finishing his journalism degree. #3707. Go fishing and fire Hornet out of a cannon in Silksong's December-bound Sea of Sorrow expansion, which Team Cherry say is "unlike anything we’ve done before"

Honest to goodness news for Hollow Knight: Silksong expansion Sea of Sorrow? That I didn’t invent in a dream? Scarcely believable, yet entirely true. The watery DLC is releasing on December 11th 2026, a scant two weeks from now, and as with original Hollow Knight's expansions it’ll be free to those who own the base game. There’s also a new trailer, showing some of the gunpowder-jumping and fishy boss-battling Hornet will get up to while exploring those sorrowful seas.

Hollow Knight: Silksong - Sea of Sorrow - Launch Trailer Watch on YouTube

Keen ramblers through Silksong’s sonorous Pharloom kingdom will note the new, aquatic locales: coral-coated ruins, damp algae forests, and bioluminescent cliffs that crackle with strange blue lighting. A piratical sub-theme also flashes up in a few places, particularly one yarr-ing jellybug boss and Hornet’s newfound talent for launching herself out of cannons as a movement aid.

There also looks to be at least another one of Silksong’s deviously tricky 'Climb a shaft while being chased by rising Bad Liquid' sections, as well as a moment when Hornet tries her claw at silk-fishing. I’m not the most accomplished Silksongist on the planet but I’ve played enough to know that whatever she catches will probably have two phases and a title card.

Or will it? In introducing the release date and trailer, as part of a Cherry Time showcase on the developers’ YouTube channel, Team Cherry claimed Sea of Sorrow is "unlike anything we’ve done before" – so further surprises are likely in store, even if I’d still wager that most of them involve needle violence. More fundamentally, Sea of Sorrow does look considerably larger in scope than any of Hollow Knight’s freebie DLCs, which at most – Godhome, basically – added a small handful of new locations and a smattering of boss challenges. Silksong’s first expansion appears to be showing off multiple new regions, legions of new enemy types, extra traversal mechanics, and that most desired of prizes among soulslike and soulslike-adjacent fans: untold lore.

And it’s out in two weeks? Time to get back in the water.

#3706. World of Warcraft: Forever's best new enchantment has been quietly changed, leaving some casters on the back foot

As World of Warcraft: Forever players dived into the game, they quickly discovered a specific weapon enchant that took area of effect spells to a whole other level. Sadly, with a sudden hotfix last night, this particular use case for the enchant has been removed.

The enchantment in question was Revelation - a new addition to the game included as part of the new trade good reputations. What it does is simple: when you fail to deal a critical strike with a spell, the next spell hit is guaranteed to do so. What made this particularly powerful is that the buff also worked with continuous area of effect spells, meaning an early instance of the spell not crit-ing would result in the remaining damage hits all dealing critical damage.

So for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell. This is a channel spell with a total of 10 seconds of cast time. Every second, it deals damage. If the first instance of damage at the one second mark doesn't crit, the remaining nine instances of damage would all crit. This resulted in absurd amounts of damage, and made players of druids, warlocks, and mages very happy.

While strong enchantments are often pricey, this was notably cheap, due to the low-cost of resources used to create it and the low requirements to learn it. As such, people were spending a handful of gold for an early game enchantment that was being actively used all the way into the end game.

It was admittedly a tad too strong, and the effect triggered on AOE spells was almost certainly an unintended effect of the enchantment. Last night, the fun came to an end. Now, the effect is used up as intended in long-casted spells. So going back to the example given, if the first instance of damage on Hurricane doesn't crit, then the second one still will. However, this will use up the effect, and the third instance of damage will revert to regular ol' damage numbers. It also seems as though it Revelation can't trigger more than once during a single channeled spell.

This is the latest in a string of ongoing quickfire bug fixes and game adjustments being made to World of Warcraft: Forever. The devs have been continuously updating the game in an attempt to curb certain gold farms, following the discovery of a particularly lucrative Blackmaw Hold gold exploit. The dev team has expressed some interesting ideas for the game longterm, including a desire to kill best-in-slot gear.

Dawn of War 4 writer John French lays out how it works.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The original Dawn of War's Winter Assault expansion added campaigns that let you play two factions at once, with different final missions based on which one you triumphed with. Dawn of War 2's campaign was even more player-led, with distress calls that had different outcomes based on what you prioritized and, in the Chaos Rising expansion, a morality mechanic with Corruption and Redemption points. It even chose a different character to be a traitor based on who gained the most Corruption by the story's end.

I asked John French, Dawn of War 4's writer and a Warhammer novelist, whether Dawn of War 4 would follow this noble tradition by having player decisions alter the plot. "The player's decisions very much change the perspectives that they'll experience the game from," he replied. "So, depending on which heroes from each faction they choose, they'll have a very different experience of the game, in that they'll see different parts of the story and sometimes different views on the same events."

Based on what we've seen of the Ork and Adeptus Mechanicus campaigns, that means partway through you'll be presented with a choice between two Commanders who have opposed goals and the one you pick will lead to missions with different objectives. Ork Beastboss Guzcutta is trying to unite his clan, the Snakebites, while his rival warboss, Gorgutz, is an off-world interloper trying to rebuild his damaged invasion force.

"With characters like Gorgutz and Guzcutta," French explained, "it can be as simple as one of them wants to do it the traditional, brutal ork way, and one of them wants to do it in a brutal but cunning way, so you have missions that focus on getting lots of shiny kit in one, while the other tries to get as many orks to follow them as possible.

"In a more complex narrative, like the Adeptus Mechanicus campaign, Potentia-Delta-9's main drive is the quest for knowledge, and she is on a very different path from Skitarii Marshal Sek-Ix-23, who is very much about enforcing the orthodoxy. The story for both overlaps, but which character you choose and what decisions you make with them lead down different experiences of an overlapping story."

Writing an RTS isn't all about plotting out the campaign missions. The Dawn of War games are legendary for their unit barks, like the saber-rattling Lord Commissar who shouts, from the top of an armored Chimera transport, "Drive me closer, I want to hit them with my sword!" Getting across so much personality in a short space is a real skill.

"You can do an awful lot with just a couple of words like 'More dakka!'," French said, "that tells you a huge amount about the orks on its own. Even with factions like the necrons, the way that the lower ranks respond to the higher ones with just 'Obedience,' one word, tells how their faction works."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Part of the appeal of Warhammer is the berserk variety of its armies, each with its own highly thematic identity. You walk into a shop and see the stoic space marines alongside spiky Chaos daemons and units of Astra Militarum who look like they stepped out of a trench in World War I before being given laser rifles.

"Dawn of War 4 is deeply Warhammer in that way because it's got all of these different textures of factions and characters next to each other," French said. "You have orks, and they are absolutely fixated on smashing everything they can in the pursuit of trying to have an even bigger fight. Then you've got the Adeptus Mechanicus, who revere machines as holy and worship the machine as god with complete sincerity and total conviction. Those two things literally exist side by side, along with alien races who have made themselves immortal by creating metal bodies with hyper advanced technology. And all of these different types of character come into conflict on one planet cut off in a sea of night—that's very Warhammer."

Dawn of War 4 is due out on December 3 and will be available on Steam. Owners of the Commander Edition will get advance access and can play from November 30.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Big Issue, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation, published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame.

#3704. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 gets a model painter demo, so you can make a mess of your Orks, Necrons, Space Marines and AdMech before they even hit the battlefield

In the grim darkness of the week before the release of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4, developers King Art and publishers Deep Silver have released a demo model painter. It's your chance to pre-emptively run a brush over units from the new strategy game's four major factions – Orks, Adeptus Mechanicus, Necrons and Space Marines. The Imperial Guard are in the game too, but mostly as a tutorial army. What a slap in the face for the Imperium's vanilla humans.

Deep Silver are calling it "the most powerful Painter in Dawn of War history", which doesn't seem all that dashing a boast given that Dawn of War 3 came out almost 10 years ago and today's PCs have a fair bit more RAM in them. You can opt for Basic Painter mode in order to quickly knock together livery for entire armies, or fire up the Advanced Painter and get stuck into the weeds of individual armour and body parts, with a choice of materials, patterns, decals and weathering. Here be trailer.

Gosh, don't your units look splendid, after literal moments of tinkering! What a colossal waste it would be to buy the full version of DOW4, import your custom designs, and watch them get all scratched and blown to pieces! Although that is obviously the idea - this is bog-standard preorder bait. You can also send your designs to other players using codes, which is nice. I plan to fashion my very own line of Space Marine chapters with colour schemes that can be deduced from the title alone: the dreaded Magpie Men, the valiant Traffic Lightbearers, and the Emperor's own Paisley Pillagers.

There is surely no greater insult for a table-top Warhammer player than having your opponent show up to the battle with an unpainted army. Somebody did this to me once, which is partly why I don't play tabletop Warhammer anymore (the main reason, of course, is that tabletop Warhammer is mind-bogglingly expensive). I'd spent hours on my own High Elves, getting the blue of the pennants and the gilt of the heraldry just right, and here's some guy with an army of grey plastic and pewter. Might as well have moulded his troops out of chewing gum and saved himself £50!

Well, there'll be no excuse for showing up with a blandly dressed army in Dawn of War 4. Find the model painter on Steam. As for the actual warmaking component of DOW4, Julian worries the devs are playing it too safe.

#3703. Why did Rockstar Games make empathy a key mechanic in GTA 6? "Because it's fun" says head of development Rob Nelson

That, and parts of RDR2 became "too hard to ignore or walk away from".

There's been plenty of chatter about Grand Theft Auto 6's 'honour system', so to speak, implemented here via what the game calls your Criminal Profile.

Our own Dom just wrote that they prefer to turn its notifications off, for instance, in favour of fully soaking into the immersion. Personally I quite like the pop-ups - I find the act of figuring out systems and how they're manipulated almost as fun as the games they're a part of. And pop-ups or no, the fact that GTA 6 can arguably be portrayed as 'rewarding' empathy and 'discouraging' the series' famous rampages of mass violence has sparked a fair bit of debate.

Some of that is genuinely interesting - I'm dubious as to whether that's really what this system is doing, for a start. Is it incentivising and disincentivising certain in-game behaviour, or just putting a label on it? And then, actually: does the act of labelling "psycho" behaviour alone actually become a disincentivising factor in itself?

Either way, until now Rockstar hasn't said a great deal about why, exactly, this system - seen by some as one that builds empathy into GTA's chaotic world - was implemented in the first place. But during an interview I had with Rob Nelson, Rockstar Games' head of development, just before GTA 6's launch earlier this month, a little more on that came to light.

A little context is necessary here: Nelson's response was actually following a question I had about the overall approach to design that Rockstar took, and how its wider themes and intentions came about. As a part of that, he turned to this system - and how, in a way, it exists here because of the work the studio simply didn't want to leave behind after Red Dead Redemption 2.

Nelson explained that this all began when the team was in the early phase of exploring what type of game GTA 6 would be, in 2015 and 2016, while much of the studio was still working full-tilt on RDR2 - a game which itself didn't release until late 2018. The team was looking to "build up the sophistication of the NPC population, and also allow for more player choice than we had [before], and more options in terms of the way you interact with the world beyond just violence," Nelson told me.

The idea would be that "it's still a world of violence - but you could threaten somebody by aiming a gun at them and just robbing them, and they have a chance to comply. So you don't have to beat them to death to get their money." Ideas that were "simple things" in principle, he said, "but they create a lot more work in terms of development of the sophistication of the systems."

Then, as systems were gradually implemented, it became a question of "trying to marry up what you're doing in the open world with who we're saying you are in the narrative - more than we had, I would say, previously, in Red Dead 2." It's here where the system now referred to as the Criminal Profile started to form.

The thinking turned to "the nature of 'honour', which wasn't always a part of it" with Red Dead Redemption 2, Nelson continued, "but became part of it as we were working on this story and finding that the 'redemption arc' didn't feel so good when it was foisted upon you - and feelings that we had playing Red Dead sort of early on." (Those feelings, primarily, were around getting you to invest in a gang led by Dutch Van der Linde, who was fundamentally unlikable from the off - or plain "crazy", as Nelson put it. The implementation of more player choices and agency was part of Rockstar's way to build investment in Arthur, even as he followed Dutch.)

That meant moving the choices away from key story moments, where many games tend to put them. Instead, Rockstar built a system that ran alongside the story via smaller, moment-to-moment choices you might make. "We tried to take all of those off the main flow and make them optional. So again, they're a choice."

"Usually they involve some form of slight sacrifice or more effort on the part of the player," he added. The hope, then, was that you as a player would both "feel something", and ultimately also feel "you got the outcome that you deserved."

That was the initial thinking behind this kind of system as a whole. Coming to GTA 6, it then combined with a wider desire to "evolve" Grand Theft Auto as both the team's storytelling and the available technology matured. "You're thinking about story and character set, but we're also thinking about what we want to do with GTA as a series, and how you want to evolve it," Nelson said.

"I think as the resolution goes up, it sort of asks different new questions," he continued. "As the resolution goes up, you want the sophistication of the experience to go up, and obviously the sophistication of the mechanics. So it just naturally flowed that we give players choices to interact with the world beyond just violence, beyond just 'down the barrel of a gun', because it's fun."

"It's fun for some people like myself to just sort of role-play in the world, and be in the world, and restraint becomes something you hadn't thought about," he continued. That tied back into the more sophisticated NPCs and reactions the team were making.

"If you think about the NPCs, even back to [GTA] 5, you would draw a weapon - first of all, they didn't react if you drew an invisible shotgun out of nowhere, or a rocket launcher," he said. "They don't react unless you aim it, and then they flee in terror, and you're just sort of this demigod stomping through the world, you know? And that's fun, but for how long?

"The team then started thinking of ways to build a bit more sustained enjoyment from it. "What if you can't do that?" Nelson continued. What if, instead of whipping an RPG out of nowhere, "you have to call your car. You have to pop a car trunk and get it, and now I'm walking, and now people are noticing, but they're sort of sidling away, and it's more believable. And then they're still fleeing in terror, but then there's people who also have guns, and they're shooting at you, or you try to hold somebody up and they pull a gun, or they grab it, and then you have to deal with them.

"And then, he continued, "you choose. You're trying to jack somebody off a motorcycle, and they pull a gun on you, and you have to blow their head off and it's like, 'You shouldn't have made me do that!' And so then it has more meaning, and it's more funny in a way when it's a little bit more pointed. And you can still go on those rampages and basically smash your Criminal Profile until it breaks and then you enter this irredeemable state, which basically says 'I reject your criminal profile system! I don't want it.'"

That Irredeemable profile level, for what it's worth, was another element born of Red Dead Redemption 2. "We had that with Red Dead, where people would sort of have low honour, and then 'greet' their way back up to high honour. And so this was an attempt of sorts of [making something] for people that just want to go crazy and almost opt out of the system. They can opt out of it - and you can also turn off the notifications in the system."

It's notable, in fact, just how interlinked the thinking was with GTA 6 and Red Dead Redemption 2. As Nelson put it at one point: "There was maybe more emotional resonance in the story of RDR2 than we had had, certainly in a GTA before. So we liked that idea." What Rockstar did with GTA 6 was then in a way a natural next step. "We didn't necessarily come to GTA 6 going: 'We must have emotional resonance,' but all of those things combine. It's more that those systems and that element of player choice and agency, and the way that affected the narrative, was a hard thing to ignore and walk away from."

We'll have much more like this from our interview with Nelson very soon, so do look out for that on Eurogamer over the coming days. In the meantime, we've a handy guide explaining exactly how GTA 6's Criminal Profile system works and how to change, raise, or lower that profile if you're in need of a deep dive into how it all really works.

The Emperor’s New Groove is one of those Walt Disney Animation movies that will forever and always be imprinted in my brain. The 2000 film came out at just the right time in my childhood when I’d put it on repeat. I could honestly quote most of it front to back. However, I had no idea about the experience Kuzco's voice actor, David Spade, had.

The animation movie landscape has changed a lot over the years. These days all the big roles go to Hollywood names rather than talents known specifically for voice acting. David Spade, who famously got his start on SNL, spoke to this while talking about The Emperor’s New Groove with these words:

I was the last guy to do a Disney movie where they said it was ‘an honor’, and that’s why I didn’t get a lot of money. And then, they came out with Shrek, and everyone got $5 million bucks, and I go 'Wait, what the fuck is going on?'

Hey, he makes a good point. Prior to the 21st Century, animated movies weren't paying big-name celebrities the big bucks. David Spade was also working with Disney Animation at a time when the studio wasn’t making blockbusters to the degree it is now with the likes of Frozen or Moana. Spade even disclosed how much he made, saying this:

I got $75,000, which sounds like a lot. It was a lot… They rat fucked me.

Shrek came out in 2001 – one year after The Emperor’s New Groove – and made almost half a billion worldwide. It helped usher in an era of blockbuster animated films led by A-list celebrities that we continue to live in. The Emperor's New Groove made $169 million worldwide, and was actually thought of as a commercial flop at the time of its release.

Spade’s comments about The Emperor’s New Groove were made while on his podcast Fly On The Wall with guest Denis Leary, who famously plays Diego the saber-tooth tiger in the Ice Age movies. Ice Age came out a couple of years after Spade’s Disney movie, and has a sixth installment among upcoming Disney movies in 2027. Leary said he and the rest of the Ice Age cast have received pay bumps since first signing up to the franchise because they are watched so frequently on streaming.

Even though I imagine it’s a bummer that Spade lost out on some cash he might have gotten for the same amount of work a couple of years later on something else, he also made a point of saying he loves The Emperor’s New Groove and how well it turned out. But he did so while pointing out something else about being a voice actor on a Disney film that was hard to deal with in the moment…

No, I did it and it just kept going and going, and I’m like, ‘Guys, I don’t want to drive out to Disney every day and just lay down an hour or two of tracks. I’m like Denis Leary, I have shit to do on my day off. I love the movie now, but during it I was starting to get a little itchy. Like, there’s no ending. I really love it, and they’re miracle workers with the freaking animation.

Animated movies like The Emperor’s New Groove famously go through a long production process. The 2000 movie in particular did so because it was actually originally an entirely different movie called Kingdom of the Sun. It was more inspired by The Prince and the Pauper, featured Owen Wilson in a voice role, and Spade was playing a character named Manco instead of Kuzco before they shifted directions. No wonder he was getting antsy while making it!

While I can understand David Spade’s blunt thoughts about working with Disney, I’m so happy he stuck it out and played Kuzco. The movie has brought me so much joy throughout my life, and it’s certainly one of the most beloved projects of his career. You can watch it now with a Disney+ subscription.

Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

#3701. Rumoured Simpsons: Hit & Run remake could be dead in the water, as New Radical Games devs suggest their unannounced game's been cancelled

Simpsons creator Matt Groening appeared to lend credence this summer to chatter about a potential return for Hit and Run

Earlier this year, New Radical Games rocked up on the scene. A successor to Simpsons: Hit & Run and Prototype studio Radical Entertainment, with original Radical co-founder Ian Wilkinson as CEO, New Radical looked to be trying to trade on some of that pedigree. So, naturally, when Simpsons creator Matt Groening seemed to indicate during a panel that Hit & Run could be making some sort of return, remake speculation began churning. Sadly, whatever New Radical were working on, it looks like that game's been cancelled.

A couple of New Radical developers have put up similar LinkedIn posts about needing to look for new work over the past week. "It seems that not even a fantastic project with an absolutely incredible team is immune from the current state of the industry right now, as what we were working on at New Radical Games (although mind-blowingly awesome) was part of a whole gaggle of cancellations," senior game designer Darren Evenson wrote. "A gaggle, I say!

"Oh, you silly suits with spreadsheets... will you EVER learn? If you don't make the game, you can't make the money... and if you don't make the money, then you don't get the power... and... well, there's more to that quote, but I digress."

"Alongside other projects, I'm sad to say our project was cancelled by the Publisher this week," fellow New Radical senior game designer Bob Churchill wrote in his own post a few days earlier than Evenson. "A huge shout out to everyone at New Radical Games. What we achieved in those four months was nothing short of amazing. I wish everyone could see it."

The comment from Groening which seemed to hint at Hit & Run making a return was made during the Disney fan convention D23 in August (thanks, VGC). "I think the original game is coming back in some form," he said, prompting current Simpsons showrunner Matt Selman to go into what seems like 'Ah bollocks, better sarkily suggest we didn't just let that slip' mode.

Assuming the right deals could feasibly be made to render it possible, a Hit & Run remake would seem like an obvious opportunity to rake in a tonne of nostalgia bank, given how many folks my age and older have fond memories of running around Springfield in it. The Simpsons' relatively recent cameos in Fortnite also seem to have gone down pretty well, suggesting the very long-running series isn't something the kids of today turn their noses up at.

Whatever these New Radical Games devs were working on, hopefully they're able to land on their feet in new work soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Square Enix's $300,000 crackdown on fake Tifa figures isn't the only anti-counterfeit operation going on among Japan's biggest game publishers. The Final Fantasy publisher has joined forces with Capcom and Bandai to take down knockoff merch, and the joint operation has already led to the seizure of around $200,000 worth of fake Gundams.

Counterfeit merch is often reported by rightsholders, but they can only make claims on goods that infringe on their IP. So while warehouses might be full of fake Final Fantasy, Street Fighter, and Gundam figures, publishers filing reports could only ask local officials to seize the merchandise directly related to their own IP.

That's why the companies decided to team up, according to a representative of the legal department of Bandai Spirits, which is Bandai Namco's toy-making subsidiary. According to a recent report from Oricon News, translated by Automaton Media, this partnership has been ongoing since July.

The three companies launched a joint crackdown against a Chinese merchandiser, which led to the arrest of the store operator and the seizure of 137 pieces of fake Gundam merch, estimated to be worth around 31 million yen, or around $194,000 USD.

Square Enix had its own merch crackdown earlier this year, ahead of this joint venture. It all kicked off with reports of fake Tifa figures, which led to 13 arrests and $300,000 worth of assets being seized. I guess next time, the fake Chun-Lis and Bulmas won't be safe, either.

#3698. The PC specs for Mass Effect-like RPG Exodus are basically bearable for a blockbuster space opera in 2026

Not sure how much RAM Matthew McConaughey requires these days

Between Matthew McConaughey, the flesh cathedrals, the space bears, FemJun and the tragedy of Biggs "The Bolt" Keil, the pre-release reveals for Mass Effect-like space RPG Exodus have been a real emotional rollercoaster. It's almost disappointing to learn that the recommended PC system specs are just sort of… fine. Broadly within expectations, by 2026 standards, anyway.

True, you'll need one of those Nvidia RTX 5080 things if you want to play it in 4K at 60fps, but the True Gamer understands that 4K/60FPS is a dangerous and blasphemical overreach, akin to building the Tower of Babel out of cats. 1080p/30FPS was perfectly good enough for Virtua Tennis 3 on Xbox 360, and it'll be perfectly good enough for this game about *squints*… octopus mercenaries. For that, you'll only need an i5-10400, an Nvidia 2060 and a mere 16GB of RAM. Granted, I think new PCs with those components currently cost $200,000, but that isn't Exodus's fault. It's that Jensen Huang who's to blame. Here's the complete spec rundown, anyway.

Will you be playing Exodus? I think it looks swankier so far than Owlcat's surprisingly unconvincing The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, that other great hope of people who mourn Mass Effect 5, but I haven't spent any time with a build. It's out 7th April 2027 - I imagine these recommended specs might alter as they stuff in more McConaughey and layer up the space bears.
